T1-001.x: Hello, teacher! The weather is nice today.
T1-001.e: Literally 'Are you at peace?' — the everyday polite hello.
T1-001.t: Works any time of day — morning, afternoon or evening. A slight bow while saying it is polite.

T1-002.forms: casual: 잘 가 · formal: 안녕히 가십시오
T1-002.t: Say 가세요 to the person who is leaving. If you leave and they stay, say 안녕히 계세요.

T1-003.forms: casual: 잘 있어 · formal: 안녕히 계십시오
T1-003.x: Thank you for the meal. Goodbye!
T1-003.e: 안녕히 (peacefully) + 계세요 (please stay) — 'stay in peace'; said by the one leaving.
T1-003.t: Used when YOU are leaving and the other person stays, e.g. leaving a shop or someone's home.

T1-004.x: Thank you so much for the gift.
T1-004.e: 감사 (thanks) + 합니다 (I do) — the formal 'thank you'.

T1-005.x: Thank you for showing me the way.
T1-005.e: From 고맙다 (to be grateful) — the native Korean partner of 감사합니다; both are polite.

T1-006.x: Sorry I'm late. The traffic was really bad.
T1-006.e: Literally 'not at ease' + 합니다 — I feel uneasy about what I did.
T1-006.t: With elders, bosses or customers, 죄송합니다 is safer and more respectful.

T1-007.forms: polite: 죄송해요 · past: 죄송했습니다 (no casual form)
T1-007.x: I'm so sorry to have kept you waiting so long.
T1-007.e: Literally 'guilty and fearful' + 합니다 — more formal than 미안합니다.
T1-007.t: More humble than 미안합니다. Use it with teachers, bosses, elders and customers.

T1-008.forms: casual: 괜찮아 · formal: 괜찮습니다 · question: 괜찮아요?
T1-008.m: it's okay, I'm fine; no thanks; not bad
T1-008.e: One word, many jobs: 'it's fine', 'no thanks', or 'not bad', depending on tone.
T1-008.t: Pronounced [괜차나요]. Also a polite 'no thanks' when offered something.

T1-009.forms: formal set phrase · friendlier: 만나서 반가워요
T1-009.m: how do you do?, nice to meet you (lit. I see you for the first time)
T1-009.x: How do you do? I'm Kim Minsu.
T1-009.e: Literally 'I will see you for the first time'; 뵙다 is the humble form of 보다 (to see).
T1-009.t: Very polite, for formal first meetings. Usually followed by your name and 잘 부탁드립니다.

T1-010.forms: polite: 만나서 반가워요 · casual: 만나서 반가워
T1-010.m: nice to meet you, glad to meet you
T1-010.x: Nice to meet you. I'm from the United States.
T1-010.e: 만나다 (to meet) + 반갑다 (glad to see someone) — 'having met you, I'm glad'.

T1-011.forms: polite: 잘 먹을게요 · casual: 잘 먹을게
T1-011.m: thank you for the meal (said before eating)
T1-011.x: Wow, it looks delicious! Thank you for the meal.
T1-011.e: Literally 'I will eat well' — said before eating, to whoever cooked or is paying.

T1-012.forms: polite: 잘 먹었어요 · casual: 잘 먹었어
T1-012.m: thank you for the meal (said after eating)
T1-012.x: Grandma, thank you — that was really delicious.
T1-012.e: Literally 'I ate well' — the past-tense partner of 잘 먹겠습니다, said after the meal.
T1-012.t: Said after eating to the host or the person who paid — also to restaurant staff when leaving.

T1-013.forms: casual: 어서 와 · formal: 어서 오십시오
T1-013.x: Welcome! How many in your party?
T1-013.e: Literally 'come quickly' — the greeting you hear walking into any Korean shop or restaurant.

T1-014.t: Only for phone calls. 여보 on its own means 'honey/dear' between spouses!

T1-015.x: Excuse me, where is the restroom?
T1-015.t: 실례지만… ('excuse me, but…') is a polite way to start a question to a stranger.

T1-016.forms: polite: 축하해요 · casual: 축하해 · humble: 축하드립니다
T1-016.x: Happy birthday! This is a present for you.

T1-017.forms: polite: 수고하셨어요 · casual: 수고했어 · leaving: 수고하세요
T1-017.m: thank you for your hard work; good work
T1-017.x: Thank you for all your hard work today. See you tomorrow.
T1-017.e: Literally 'you received hardship' — thanks for the effort.
T1-017.t: Common at the end of a workday or task. When leaving a shop, people often say 수고하세요.

T1-018.m: just a moment, wait a second; excuse me (passing through)
T1-018.x: Wait a second, I didn't bring my wallet.

T1-019.e: 예 is a slightly more formal 'yes'.
T1-019.t: 네? with a rising tone means 'Sorry? / Pardon?'. Also used just to show you're listening.

T1-020.forms: short: 아뇨 · casual: 아니 · formal: 아닙니다
T1-020.e: From 아니다 (to not be); often shortened to 아뇨, and casually just 아니.
T1-020.t: Don't mix it up with 아니에요 ('it isn't' / 'not at all'), the usual reply to 감사합니다.

T1-021.forms: subject: 제가 · object: 저를 · my: 제 (제 이름)
T1-021.ex: 제 이름은 마이클이에요. 저는 미국 사람이에요.
T1-021.x: My name is Michael. I'm American.
T1-021.t: Use 저 whenever you speak politely. With 가 it becomes 제가, never 저가.

T1-022.forms: subject: 내가 · object: 나를 · my: 내 (내 친구)
T1-022.e: Casual 'I' (humble: 저); becomes 내가 before 가, and 내 = my.

T1-023.e: Humble version of 우리 — use with elders or customers: 저희 회사 'our company'.
T1-023.t: 저희 excludes the listener. For 'our country', always say 우리나라, never 저희 나라.

T1-024.t: Koreans say 우리 where English says 'my': 우리 엄마 (my mom), 우리 집 (my home).

T1-025.forms: subject: 네가 (spoken 니가) · object: 너를 · your: 네 (네 책)
T1-025.x: My friend asked, 'Where are you right now?'
T1-025.e: Becomes 네가 before 가 — usually pronounced 니가 so it doesn't sound like 내가 (I).
T1-025.t: Only for close friends your age or younger people. With others, use their name or title instead of 'you'.

T1-026.t: In speech 이것 usually becomes 이거: 이거 얼마예요? (How much is this?)

T1-027.e: 그 (that) + 것 (thing); in speech usually 그거.

T1-028.x: What building is that over there?
T1-028.e: 저 (that over there) + 것 (thing); in speech usually 저거.

T1-029.x: This is the school I go to.
T1-029.e: Same 이/그/저 pattern: 여기 (here), 거기 (there), 저기 (over there).
T1-029.t: 여기요! is also a common way to call a waiter in a restaurant.

T1-030.x: Please wait there. I'll come to you.
T1-030.e: Same 이/그/저 pattern: 여기 (here), 거기 (there), 저기 (over there).

T1-031.m: over there; um, excuse me (to get attention)
T1-031.x: The restroom is over there on the right.
T1-031.e: Same 이/그/저 pattern as 여기, 거기.
T1-031.t: 저기요! is the usual way to say 'Excuse me!' to a stranger or a waiter.

T1-032.forms: subject: 누가 (not 누구가) · object: 누구를 (누굴) · whose: 누구의
T1-032.x: Who is this person in the photo?
T1-032.t: With 가, 누구 becomes 누가: 누가 왔어요? (Who came?)

T1-033.x: What did you do last weekend?
T1-033.e: Mostly heard in its short spoken form 뭐; 무엇을 shortens to 뭘.
T1-033.t: 무엇 is written or formal; in conversation people almost always say 뭐.

T1-034.x: What do you want to eat for lunch?
T1-034.e: Spoken short form of 무엇: 뭐예요? 'What is it?'; 뭐 해요? 'What are you doing?'

T1-035.e: 어디 가요? 'Where are you going?' is a casual greeting in Korea, not nosiness.

T1-036.e: Add 나 and get 언제나 'always'; 언제든지 = 'anytime'.

T1-037.x: Why didn't you come to school yesterday?
T1-037.e: Sounds like English 'way', but means 'why': 왜요? 'Why?'
T1-037.t: Politely ask 왜요? A bare 왜? can sound blunt to elders.

T1-038.forms: 어떻게 해요? (what should I do?) · from 어떻다 (to be how)
T1-038.x: How do I get from here to Seoul Station?
T1-038.t: Pronounced [어떠케]. 어떡해! ('What do I do?!') is a common exclamation.

T1-039.x: How much is one of these apples?
T1-039.e: 얼마예요? 'How much is it?'; 얼마나 = 'how much / how long'.

T1-040.forms: 몇 + counter: 몇 개 · 몇 살 · 몇 시 · 몇 명
T1-040.x: Excuse me, what time is it now?
T1-040.e: Used with counters: 몇 개 (how many things), 몇 살 (how old), 몇 시 (what time).
T1-040.t: 'What date' is spelled 며칠, never 몇 일. Pronounced [멷].

T1-041.forms: 어느 + noun: 어느 나라 · 어느 것 (어느 거) · 어느 쪽
T1-041.e: 어느 나라 사람이에요? 'Which country are you from?' — a classic first question.

T1-042.forms: 무슨 + noun: 무슨 요일 · 무슨 일 · 무슨 음식
T1-042.x: What day of the week is it today?
T1-042.e: 무슨 일이에요? 'What's going on?'; 무슨 요일 = 'what day of the week'.

T1-043.forms: 어떤 + noun: 어떤 사람 · 어떤 음식 · from 어떻다
T1-043.m: what kind of, what sort of; which; a certain, some
T1-043.x: What kind of music do you like?
T1-043.e: From 어떻다 (to be how) — same family as 어떻게 (how).
T1-043.t: 어떤 asks about qualities ('what is it like?'); 무슨 asks about type or identity.

T1-044.forms: 이 + noun: 이 사람 · 이 책 · 이것 (this thing) · 여기 (here)
T1-044.e: 이/그/저 = this / that (near you) / that over there. Homonyms: 이 also means tooth and two.

T1-045.forms: 그 + noun: 그 사람 · 그 영화 · 그것 (that thing) · 거기 (there)
T1-045.m: that (near the listener, or already mentioned); the
T1-045.x: Have you seen that movie? It's really good.
T1-045.e: Also builds 그것 (that) and 거기 (there); in writing 그 can mean 'he'.

T1-046.forms: 저 + noun: 저 사람 · 저 건물 · 저것 (that thing) · 저기 (over there)
T1-046.x: That person over there is our teacher.
T1-046.t: Same spelling as 저 'I (humble)'. Before a noun it means 'that over there'.

T1-047.forms: 사람이 · 사람을 · honorific: 분 · plural: 사람들
T1-047.x: There are so many people in the park.
T1-047.e: Add it to a country for nationality: 한국 사람 (Korean), 미국 사람 (American).

T1-048.forms: 분이 · 분을 · plain: 사람 · 이분 · 몇 분
T1-048.x: That gentleman is the president of our company.
T1-048.e: Polite word for 사람: 이분 'this person'. Watch out: 분 also means 'minute'.
T1-048.t: Restaurant staff ask 몇 분이세요? (How many people?). Don't use 분 for yourself. Not to be confused with 분 'minute'.

T1-049.x: I watched a movie with a friend on the weekend.
T1-049.e: Literally 'close and old' — an old, close companion.
T1-049.t: 친구 usually means someone the same age. Older friends are called 형, 오빠, 누나 or 언니.

T1-050.x: That man is my older brother.

T1-051.x: There are more girls in our class.

T1-052.forms: 아이가 · 아이를 · short: 애 · plural: 아이들
T1-052.x: The child is playing in the park.
T1-052.e: Often shortened to 애 in speech; 아이들 = children.

T1-053.x: You should use polite speech with elders.
T1-053.e: Also 'elder' — showing respect to 어른 is a big part of Korean manners.

T1-054.e: Literally 'learning life' — someone whose life is learning.
T1-054.t: Pronounced [학쌩]: ㅅ after a ㄱ batchim becomes tense ㅆ.

T1-055.e: Literally 'born before' + 님 (honorific) — someone who is ahead of you.
T1-055.t: Also a respectful title for doctors and other professionals. Use honorific verbs: 선생님이 오세요.

T1-056.t: To elders, ask politely: 성함이 어떻게 되세요?

T1-057.x: Excuse me, but may I ask how old you are?
T1-057.e: Koreans often ask your 나이 early because it decides who speaks politely to whom.
T1-057.t: Age matters in Korea because it decides speech level. For elders, use 연세: 연세가 어떻게 되세요?

T1-058.x: Some guests are coming to my house this evening.
T1-058.e: 손 (old word for guest) + 님 (honorific) — not related to 손 'hand'.

T1-059.x: The owner of this restaurant is very kind.

T1-060.x: There are a lot of foreigners in Seoul these days.
T1-060.e: Literally 'outside-country person'. Add -인 to a country for its people: 미국인 = American.

T1-061.x: There are four people in my family.
T1-061.e: Literally 'house clan' — the people under one roof.

T1-062.forms: 아버지가 · 아버지를 · honorific: 아버님 · casual: 아빠
T1-062.x: My father works at a bank.
T1-062.e: Casual form 아빠 (dad); add 할 and get 할아버지 (grandfather).
T1-062.t: Use honorific verbs for parents: 아버지께서 주무세요 (Father is sleeping).

T1-063.forms: 어머니가 · 어머니를 · honorific: 어머님 · casual: 엄마
T1-063.e: Casual form 엄마 (mom); 할머니 (grandmother) is built on it.

T1-064.x: Dad, are you coming home early today?
T1-064.e: Casual word for 아버지 — many adults keep using it too.

T1-065.x: Mom made kimchi stew for me.
T1-065.e: Casual word for 어머니 — sounds like 'mama' in many languages.

T1-066.x: I call my parents every weekend.

T1-067.x: My grandfather lives in the countryside.
T1-067.t: Pronounced [하라버지]. Also a polite way to address any elderly man.

T1-068.x: My grandmother gave me rice cakes.
T1-068.e: 할 (great) + 어머니 (mother), shortened; also used for any elderly woman.

T1-069.m: older brother (of a male); older male friend (of a male)
T1-069.x: My older brother is a university student.
T1-069.t: Only males say 형. Females call an older brother 오빠.

T1-070.m: older brother (of a female); older male friend (of a female)
T1-070.x: My older brother is three years older than me.
T1-070.e: In K-dramas also for male idols.
T1-070.t: Only females say 오빠. It's also used for an older boyfriend or a close older male friend.

T1-071.m: older sister (of a male); older female friend (of a male)
T1-071.x: My older sister works at a company.
T1-071.t: Only males say 누나. Females call an older sister 언니.

T1-072.m: older sister (of a female); older female friend (of a female)
T1-072.x: I went shopping with my older sister.
T1-072.e: Used only by females; also a friendly way to address a young woman at a shop.

T1-073.x: My younger sibling is a high school student.
T1-073.e: Literally 'same birth'; add 남 or 여 for brother or sister: 남동생, 여동생.

T1-075.x: My younger sister sings really well.

T1-076.x: Do you have any brothers or sisters?

T1-077.x: Our son is seven years old this year.
T1-077.e: Paired with 딸: 아들딸 = 'sons and daughters'.

T1-078.e: Paired with 아들: 아들딸 = 'sons and daughters'.

T1-079.forms: 남편이 · 남편을 · honorific: 남편분 (someone else's husband)
T1-079.x: My husband is an office worker.
T1-079.t: Talking about someone else's husband politely, say 남편분.

T1-080.forms: 아내가 · 아내를 · honorific: 부인 (someone else's wife)
T1-080.x: I go to the market with my wife.
T1-080.e: Use 아내 for your own wife.
T1-080.t: For someone else's wife, use 부인 or 사모님. In casual speech many people also say 와이프.

T1-081.x: The baby is sleeping in the room.
T1-081.t: In speech you often hear 애기, but the standard spelling is 아기.

T1-082.t: 'Marry someone' uses 와/과 or 하고, not 을/를: 친구하고 결혼했어요. Pronounced [겨론].

T1-083.forms: native · counting things, hours, age · before a counter: 한 (한 개, 한 시)
T1-083.t: Before a counter 하나 shortens to 한: 한 명, 한 살, 한 시.

T1-084.forms: native · counting things, hours, age · before a counter: 두 (두 개, 두 시)
T1-084.t: Before a counter 둘 becomes 두: 두 사람, 두 잔.

T1-085.forms: native · counting things, hours, age · before a counter: 세 (세 개, 세 시)
T1-085.x: There are three of us in my family.
T1-085.t: Before a counter 셋 becomes 세: 세 명, 세 시.

T1-086.forms: native · counting things, hours, age · before a counter: 네 (네 개, 네 시)
T1-086.x: There are four people in the room.
T1-086.t: Before a counter 넷 becomes 네: 네 명, 네 시.

T1-087.forms: native · counting things, hours, age · same before a counter (다섯 개, 다섯 시)
T1-087.e: Native numbers count things and ages: 다섯 살 = five years old.

T1-088.forms: native · counting things, hours, age · same before a counter (여섯 개, 여섯 시)
T1-088.x: Our son is six years old.
T1-088.e: Don't mix up 여섯 (6) and 여덟 (8) — both start with 여.
T1-088.t: Final ㅅ sounds like ㄷ: 여섯 [여섣], 여섯 시 [여섣씨].

T1-089.forms: native · counting things, hours, age · same before a counter (일곱 개, 일곱 시)
T1-089.x: I get up at seven in the morning.
T1-089.e: Not related to Sino-Korean 일 (one) — 일곱 is seven. 일곱 시 = 7 o'clock.

T1-090.forms: native · counting things, hours, age · same before a counter (여덟 개, 여덟 시)
T1-090.x: Eight friends came to the party.
T1-090.t: Pronounced [여덜]: the ㅂ in the ㄼ batchim is silent.

T1-091.forms: native · counting things, hours, age · same before a counter (아홉 개, 아홉 시)
T1-091.e: Hours use native numbers: 아홉 시 = 9 o'clock.

T1-092.forms: native · counting things, hours, age · 11–19: 열하나, 열둘 … (열한 개, 열두 시)
T1-092.e: Homonym: 열 also means heat or fever (열이 나요 = I have a fever).
T1-092.t: Teens combine 열 + number: 열하나 (11), 열둘 (12). Before counters: 열한 시, 열두 시.

T1-093.forms: native · counting things, age · before a counter: 스무 (스무 살) · 21+: 스물한 살
T1-093.x: My younger sibling is twenty years old.
T1-093.t: Alone before a counter it becomes 스무: 스무 살. With a unit digit it stays 스물: 스물두 살.

T1-094.forms: native · counting things, age · same before a counter (서른 살, 서른한 명)
T1-094.x: My older sister is thirty this year.
T1-094.e: Common for ages: 서른 살 = 30 years old.

T1-095.forms: native · counting things, age · same before a counter (마흔 살, 마흔두 명)
T1-095.x: My uncle is forty this year.
T1-095.e: Native tens are separate words to memorize: 스물 20, 서른 30, 마흔 40, 쉰 50.

T1-096.forms: native · counting things, age · same before a counter (쉰 살, 쉰다섯 명)
T1-096.x: My mother is fifty this year.
T1-096.t: Native tens go on: 예순 60, 일흔 70, 여든 80, 아흔 90. For larger numbers Sino-Korean is far more common.

T1-097.forms: Sino-Korean · dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, floors (일 층, 일월 일일)
T1-097.e: Also used for phone numbers. 일월 = January. Different from 일 (work).
T1-097.t: Use 일 for dates, money and minutes; use 하나/한 for counting items, people and hours.

T1-098.forms: Sino-Korean · dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, floors (이 층, 이월)
T1-098.x: My room is on the second floor.
T1-098.e: Homonyms: 이 also means 'this' and 'tooth' — context tells you which.
T1-098.t: Don't mix it up with 이 'this' or the subject particle 이 — context makes it clear.

T1-099.forms: Sino-Korean · dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, floors (삼 층, 삼월)

T1-100.forms: Sino-Korean · dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, floors (사 층, 사월)
T1-100.x: Lots of flowers bloom in April.
T1-100.e: Considered unlucky, like 13 in the US.
T1-100.t: The number 4 (사) sounds like the word for 'death', so some elevators show F instead of 4 for the fourth floor.

T1-101.forms: Sino-Korean · dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, floors (오 분, 오월)

T1-102.forms: Sino-Korean · dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, floors (육 층) · June: 유월
T1-102.x: Our home is on the sixth floor.
T1-102.t: June is 유월, not 육월. 16 (십육) is pronounced [심뉵].

T1-103.forms: Sino-Korean · dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, floors (칠 층, 칠월)

T1-104.forms: Sino-Korean · dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, floors (팔 층, 팔월)
T1-104.x: I'm going to the sea in August.

T1-105.forms: Sino-Korean · dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, floors (구 층, 구월)
T1-105.t: Homonym: 구 also means a city district, e.g. 강남구.

T1-106.forms: Sino-Korean · dates, money, minutes (십 분, 십일, 이십) · October: 시월
T1-106.e: Build bigger numbers: 십일 = 11, 이십 = 20, 이십오 = 25.

T1-107.forms: Sino-Korean · money, large numbers (백 원, 오백, 백만)

T1-108.forms: Sino-Korean · money, large numbers (천 원, 삼천, 천만)
T1-108.e: 천 원 = 1,000 won, the smallest Korean bill.

T1-109.forms: Sino-Korean · money, large numbers (만 원, 십만, 백만)
T1-109.t: Korean groups big numbers by 10,000: 100,000 = 십만, 1,000,000 = 백만.

T1-110.forms: Sino-Korean · scores, temperatures, decimals · in phone numbers: 공
T1-110.x: It's zero degrees today, so it's really cold.
T1-110.t: In phone numbers say 공 instead: 010 = 공일공.

T1-111.forms: native number + 개: 사과 세 개
T1-111.e: The all-purpose counter: 사과 한 개 = one apple. Different from 개 (dog).
T1-111.t: When you don't know the right counter for an object, 개 usually works.

T1-112.forms: native number + 명: 학생 다섯 명
T1-112.ex: 우리 반에 학생이 열 명 있어요.
T1-112.x: There are ten students in our class.
T1-112.e: Literally 'name' — you count people by names: 학생 세 명. Polite version: 분.
T1-112.t: For people you respect, use 분 instead: 손님 세 분 = three guests.

T1-113.forms: native number + 마리: 고양이 두 마리
T1-113.ex: 우리 집에는 강아지가 한 마리 있어요.
T1-113.x: We have one puppy at our house.
T1-113.e: For animals and fish: 고양이 두 마리 = two cats. Chicken places sell chicken by the 마리 (whole bird).

T1-114.forms: native number + 권: 책 세 권
T1-114.x: I borrowed two books from the library.
T1-114.e: Originally 'scroll'; 책 두 권 = two books.

T1-115.forms: native number + 장: 종이 한 장 · 표 두 장
T1-115.m: sheet(s) (counter for flat things: paper, tickets, photos)
T1-115.e: For flat things: 표 한 장 = one ticket.
T1-115.t: Also used for tickets, photos, cards, and even shirts or T-shirts.

T1-116.forms: native number + 병: 물 한 병 · 맥주 두 병
T1-116.e: Also the noun 'bottle': 물 한 병 = a bottle of water.
T1-116.t: Don't confuse with 병 (病) 'illness', as in 병원 'hospital'.

T1-117.forms: native number + 잔: 커피 한 잔 · 물 두 잔
T1-117.e: 커피 한 잔 = a cup of coffee.
T1-117.t: 한잔하다 means 'to have a drink', usually alcohol: 오늘 한잔해요!

T1-118.forms: native number + 살: 한 살 · 스무 살
T1-118.e: 살 also means flesh, as in 삼겹살.
T1-118.t: Use native numbers: 한 살, 스무 살. Forms and documents use Sino-Korean + 세: 25세.

T1-119.forms: native number + 번 = times (세 번) · Sino number + 번 = number (삼 번)
T1-119.t: 두 번 = twice; 이 번 = number two. 3번 버스 = bus No. 3.

T1-120.forms: native number + 시: 한 시 · 세 시 · 열두 시
T1-120.t: Hours use native numbers, minutes use Sino-Korean: 세 시 삼십 분 = 3:30.

T1-121.forms: Sino-Korean number + 분: 십 분 · 삼십 분
T1-121.x: It takes fifteen minutes from home to school.
T1-121.e: Minutes use Sino numbers: 세 시 십 분 = 3:10.
T1-121.t: Homonym: 분 is also the honorific counter for people — 두 분 = two (respected) people.

T1-122.forms: Sino-Korean number + 원: 천 원 · 만 원
T1-122.e: Originally 'round', for round coins — same root as Japanese yen and Chinese yuan.
T1-122.t: Ask prices with 얼마예요? 10,000원 is 만 원, not 일만 원.

T1-123.forms: Sino-Korean number + 층: 일 층 · 삼 층 · 지하 일 층
T1-123.x: The restroom is on the second floor.
T1-123.e: 삼 층 = 3rd floor. 일 층 is the ground floor, like in the US.
T1-123.t: Floors use Sino-Korean numbers. B1 = 지하 일 층. Ask: 몇 층이에요?

T1-124.forms: native number + 대: 자동차 두 대 · 컴퓨터 한 대
T1-124.ex: 우리 집에는 차가 한 대 있어요.
T1-124.x: We have one car at home.
T1-124.e: For cars and machines: 차 두 대 = two cars.
T1-124.t: Also used for phones, TVs, bicycles and other devices.

T1-125.forms: native number + 그릇: 밥 한 그릇 · 냉면 두 그릇 · noun: 그릇이 · 그릇을
T1-125.e: 밥 한 그릇 = one bowl of rice; also the everyday noun for a bowl or dish.
T1-125.t: Also a normal noun: 그릇을 씻어요 = I wash the dishes.

T1-126.forms: native number + 벌: 옷 한 벌 · 바지 두 벌
T1-126.m: counter for clothes (an outfit, a garment, a suit)
T1-126.x: I bought two outfits at the department store.
T1-126.e: 옷 한 벌 = one outfit or garment. Homonym: 벌 also means bee.

T1-127.forms: native number + 켤레: 신발 한 켤레 · 양말 두 켤레
T1-127.x: Three pairs of socks are 5,000 won.
T1-127.e: For things that come in pairs: 양말 한 켤레 = one pair of socks.

T1-128.forms: 시간이 · 시간을 · duration: 한 시간, 두 시간
T1-128.x: Do you have time on the weekend?
T1-128.e: Literally 'time span'; used with native numbers.
T1-128.t: 두 시간 = two hours (duration); 두 시 = two o'clock.

T1-129.forms: 오늘이 · 오늘은 · also used as an adverb (오늘 뭐 해요?)
T1-129.e: 오늘, 어제, 모레 are native; 내일 (tomorrow) is the odd one out — it's Sino-Korean.
T1-129.t: Can stand alone without a particle: 오늘 바빠요? = Are you busy today?

T1-130.forms: 어제가 · 어제는 · also used as an adverb (어제 갔어요)
T1-130.e: Also 어저께 in speech; 그저께 = the day before yesterday.

T1-131.forms: 내일이 · 내일은 · also used as an adverb (내일 가요)

T1-132.x: I have a test the day after tomorrow.
T1-132.e: 내일 = tomorrow, 모레 = the day after; 글피 = the day after that.

T1-133.t: 아침, 점심, 저녁 are both times of day and meals: 아침 먹었어요? = Did you eat breakfast?

T1-134.e: Same word as Chinese 'dim sum' — originally a light snack, now lunch. Just learn it whole.

T1-135.x: Let's watch a movie together this evening.
T1-135.t: Like 아침, it also means the meal: 저녁 먹었어요? = Did you have dinner?

T1-136.e: 밤 'chestnut' is said with a longer vowel.

T1-137.e: 낮 (day) vs 밤 (night); 낮잠 = nap, literally 'day sleep'.

T1-138.forms: 오전이 · 오전을 · before a time: 오전 아홉 시
T1-138.x: I have Korean class in the morning.
T1-138.t: 오전/오후 go before the time: 오전 열 시 = 10 a.m.

T1-139.forms: 오후가 · 오후를 · before a time: 오후 세 시

T1-140.m: dawn, early morning (the hours after midnight)
T1-140.x: I went to bed at 2 a.m. last night.
T1-140.t: 새벽 covers roughly midnight to sunrise: 새벽 한 시 = 1 a.m.

T1-141.x: Today is a really good day.
T1-141.e: Marks special days: 생일날 (birthday), 어린이날 (Children's Day).
T1-141.t: Useful phrases: 어느 날 'one day', 다음 날 'the next day'.

T1-142.forms: 주가 · 주를 · 이번 주 · 다음 주 · 지난주
T1-142.x: I'm going on a trip next week.
T1-142.e: 이번 주 = this week, 다음 주 = next week, 지난주 = last week.
T1-142.t: For a duration use 일주일 (one week) or 이 주 (two weeks).

T1-143.x: What are you doing on the weekend?
T1-143.e: Literally 'week end' — same idea as English.

T1-144.x: On weekdays I go to work.
T1-144.e: Literally 'ordinary day' — the opposite of 주말 (weekend).

T1-145.forms: Sino-Korean number + 월: 일월 … 십이월 · irregular: 유월 (June), 시월 (October)
T1-145.e: Months are number + 월: 일월 = January.
T1-145.t: June = 유월, October = 시월. 'What month?' = 몇 월, pronounced [며둴].

T1-146.forms: Sino-Korean number + 년: 이천이십육 년 · 일 년
T1-146.ex: 저는 한국에서 일 년 동안 살았어요.
T1-146.x: I lived in Korea for one year.
T1-146.e: Sino numbers + 년; 'this year' uses the native word 올해.
T1-146.t: After a number it's 년 (2026년); at the start of a word it becomes 연, as in 연말 'year-end'.

T1-147.e: Sun and year: one trip around the sun. 올해 = this year, 새해 = New Year.
T1-147.t: 해 also means 'sun': 해가 떠요 = The sun rises. Count years with native numbers: 한 해, 두 해.

T1-148.forms: 달이 · 달을 · 이번 달 · 다음 달 · 한 달
T1-148.x: I'm going to Korea next month.
T1-148.e: Moon and month — like English 'moon' and 'month'. 이번 달 = this month.
T1-148.t: Count months as native + 달 (한 달, 두 달) or Sino-Korean + 개월 (일 개월).

T1-149.x: What day of the week is it today?
T1-149.e: Each weekday is named after the sun, the moon, or one of five planets.
T1-149.t: Day of the week: 무슨 요일이에요? Date: 며칠이에요?

T1-150.x: I go to school on Monday.

T1-151.x: I have Korean class on Tuesday.
T1-151.e: 'Fire day' — named for Mars, the fire planet.

T1-152.x: I'm meeting a friend on Wednesday evening.
T1-152.e: 'Water day' — named for Mercury, the water planet.

T1-153.x: I have a test on Thursday.
T1-153.e: 'Wood day' — named for Jupiter, the wood planet.

T1-154.x: I watch a movie on Friday night.
T1-154.e: 'Gold day' — named for Venus, the metal planet.
T1-154.t: Pronounced [그묘일]. Slang 불금 ('fiery Friday') = a fun Friday night out.

T1-155.x: I go shopping with a friend on Saturday.
T1-155.e: 'Earth day' — named for Saturn, the earth planet.

T1-156.x: On Sundays I rest at home.

T1-157.e: Sino-Korean, literally 'just now' — today it simply means 'now'.
T1-157.t: Often used like an adverb with no particle: 지금 가요 'I'm going now'.

T1-158.forms: 이번이 · 이번에 · 이번 주 · 이번 달
T1-158.m: this time; this (coming/current) — week, month etc.
T1-158.x: I'm meeting a friend this weekend.
T1-158.t: 이번 주 = this week, 다음 주 = next week, 지난주 = last week.

T1-159.forms: 다음이 · 다음에 · 다음 주 · 다음 달
T1-159.x: Get off at the next stop.
T1-159.e: 다음 주 = next week, 다음 달 = next month.
T1-159.t: 다음에 봐요! 'See you next time!' is a common goodbye.

T1-160.forms: 지난 + time noun: 지난주 · 지난달 · 지난해
T1-160.x: I watched a movie last weekend.
T1-160.e: From 지나다 (to pass): 지난주 = last week, 지난달 = last month.
T1-160.t: Always comes before a noun. 지난주 and 지난달 are written as one word.

T1-161.t: 매 + time word means 'every': 매주 every week, 매달 every month, 매년 every year.

T1-162.e: Built on 날 (day). Don't mix it up with 날씨 (weather).
T1-162.t: To ask today's date: 오늘 며칠이에요? (not 몇 일).

T1-163.t: Say 생일 축하해요! 'Happy birthday!' Use 생신 for elders' birthdays.

T1-164.x: Lots of flowers bloom in spring.
T1-164.e: The four seasons in order: 봄, 여름, 가을, 겨울.

T1-165.x: Summer in Korea is very hot.

T1-166.x: The weather is cool in autumn.
T1-166.e: Harvest season — 추석, the Korean Thanksgiving, falls in 가을.

T1-168.e: Both parts mean 'season'. 사계절 = the four seasons.
T1-168.t: Often pronounced [게절]: ㅖ after a consonant usually sounds like ㅔ.

T1-169.t: 방학 is only for students/schools; workers take 휴가.

T1-170.forms: 휴가가 · 휴가를 · 휴가를 가다 (go on vacation)
T1-170.x: I'm going on vacation this summer.
T1-170.t: 휴가 is time off from work or the military; for school breaks use 방학.

T1-171.forms: noun + 전에 (두 시 전에) · verb + -기 전에 (자기 전에)
T1-171.x: I read a book before going to bed.
T1-171.e: Goes after the time or noun: 수업 전 = before class.
T1-171.t: With time spans it means 'ago': 삼 년 전에 = three years ago.

T1-172.forms: noun + 후에 (수업 후에) · verb + -(으)ㄴ 후에 (먹은 후에)
T1-172.x: Let's have lunch together after class.
T1-172.e: Goes after the time or noun: 수업 후 = after class.
T1-172.t: With time spans: 한 시간 후에 = in one hour (one hour later). 뒤에 is a native synonym.

T1-173.forms: noun + 동안 (일주일 동안) · verb + -는 동안 (자는 동안)
T1-173.m: during, for (a period of time), while
T1-173.x: I studied Korean during the vacation.
T1-173.t: Use with a length of time: 두 시간 동안 = for two hours.

T1-174.forms: noun + 때 (방학 때) · verb + -(으)ㄹ 때 (어릴 때)
T1-174.x: I lived in Busan when I was young.
T1-174.e: 어릴 때 = when I was young. Heads-up: 때 also means dirt or grime.
T1-174.t: -(으)ㄹ 때 means 'when ~': 시간이 있을 때 = when I have time.

T1-175.forms: attached to numbers/time: 세 시쯤 · 열 명쯤 · 일주일쯤
T1-175.x: I go home around seven o'clock.
T1-175.e: Attach it to numbers and times: 세 시쯤 = around three o'clock.
T1-175.t: Attach directly with no space: 세 시쯤, not 세 시 쯤.

T1-176.ex: 저는 오후 여섯 시에 집에 가요.
T1-176.x: I go home at six in the evening.
T1-176.e: Also means 'shop' in compounds: 빵집 (bakery), 꽃집 (flower shop).
T1-176.t: 집에 is pronounced [지베]: the batchim ㅂ moves to the next syllable.

T1-177.ex: 저는 아침 여덟 시에 학교에 가요.
T1-177.x: I go to school at eight in the morning.
T1-177.t: Pronounced [학꾜]: ㄱ after a ㄱ batchim becomes tense ㄲ.

T1-178.x: My father works at a company.
T1-178.e: Literally 'meeting company' — people gathered for business.
T1-178.t: 회사에 다니다 (lit. 'go to a company') is the usual way to say someone works at a company.

T1-179.x: My stomach hurt, so I went to the doctor.
T1-179.e: Literally 'sickness institute' — used for small clinics too.
T1-179.t: Koreans say 병원에 가다 even for a small clinic visit — it isn't as serious as 'hospital' in English.

T1-180.x: I bought cold medicine at the pharmacy.

T1-181.x: I withdrew money at the bank.
T1-181.e: Literally 'silver firm' — from the days when money meant silver.
T1-181.t: In fast speech it sounds like [으냉]: ㅎ between sounds is weak and often dropped.

T1-182.x: I sent a package at the post office.

T1-183.x: I bought fruit at the market with my mother.
T1-183.t: Homonym: 시장 (市長) also means 'mayor'. Context makes it clear.

T1-184.ex: 이 가게는 밤 열 시에 문을 닫아요.
T1-184.e: Probably from an old word meaning 'makeshift house' — a simple street stall.

T1-185.x: I bought clothes at the department store.
T1-185.e: Literally 'hundred-goods store' — a store that sells everything.
T1-185.t: Pronounced [배콰점]: ㄱ + ㅎ merge into ㅋ.

T1-186.x: I bought water at the convenience store.
T1-186.e: 편의 (convenience) + 점 (store) — 'convenience store' word for word.
T1-186.t: Pronounced [펴니점]: 의 in a non-initial syllable sounds like 이.

T1-187.x: I do grocery shopping at the supermarket on weekends.
T1-187.e: From English 'mart'. Means a big supermarket, not a small corner shop.

T1-188.x: I eat lunch at the restaurant in front of the school.
T1-188.t: Pronounced [식땅]. To call the server: 여기요!

T1-189.x: I drank coffee with a friend at a café.
T1-189.e: From French/English 'café'. Online, 카페 also means a community forum (like Naver Café).

T1-190.x: I borrowed a book from the library.
T1-190.e: Literally 'book building'. -관 = building, as in 영화관 (movie theater).

T1-191.x: I bought a Korean book at the bookstore.
T1-191.e: Literally 'book store'. -점 = store, as in 편의점 (convenience store).

T1-192.x: I take a walk in the park in the evening.

T1-193.x: I saw a movie at the theater on the weekend.
T1-193.t: 극장 is also very common for 'movie theater'.

T1-194.x: It takes an hour by bus to the airport.

T1-195.x: There's a subway station near my house.
T1-195.e: Stations are named 'X역', e.g. 서울역 (Seoul Station).
T1-195.t: Add it after a name: 강남역 = Gangnam Station. Bus stops are 정류장, not 역.

T1-196.x: I'm waiting for my friend at the bus stop.
T1-196.e: Literally 'stop-and-stay place'. 버스 정류장 = bus stop.
T1-196.t: Pronounced [정뉴장]: ㄹ after ㅇ becomes ㄴ.

T1-197.x: We stayed at a hotel near the sea.

T1-198.x: I go to church every Sunday.
T1-198.t: 교회 usually means a Protestant church; a Catholic church is 성당.

T1-199.x: I got my hair cut at the hair salon.
T1-199.e: 미용 (beauty care) + 실 (room). -실 = room, as in 교실 (classroom).
T1-199.t: 머리를 잘랐어요 is used even when someone else cut it — 'I got a haircut.'

T1-200.e: Literally 'makeup room', like English 'powder room'. 화장 alone means makeup.
T1-200.t: 화장실이 어디예요? is one of the most useful phrases for travelers.

T1-201.x: The students are studying in the classroom.

T1-202.x: My room is small but clean.
T1-202.e: -방 = room for an activity: 노래방 (karaoke, 'song room'), PC방 (internet café).

T1-203.x: My mother is cooking in the kitchen.
T1-203.t: Pronounced [부억] alone, but 부엌에 → [부어케]: the ㅋ links to the next vowel.

T1-204.x: My family is watching TV in the living room.
T1-204.e: Literally 'living room' — word for word like English!

T1-205.x: The office is on the third floor.
T1-205.t: 사무실 is the physical room; 회사 is the company itself.

T1-206.e: Native word for country. Country names use the Sino-Korean 국 instead, as in 한국.
T1-206.t: Koreans call Korea 우리나라 'our country', written as one word.

T1-207.x: I came to Korea last year.
T1-207.t: Add 사람 for people (한국 사람) and 어/말 for language (한국어, 한국말).

T1-208.x: My friend is from the U.S.
T1-208.e: 미 comes from an old sound-spelling of 'America'; the character also means 'beautiful'.

T1-210.x: I'm going to Japan this vacation.
T1-210.e: Literally 'sun origin' — the land of the rising sun.

T1-211.x: It rains often in the UK.
T1-211.e: 영 comes from an old sound-spelling of 'England'.

T1-212.e: A sound-spelling of 'Deutsch' — the parts' meanings don't matter. 독일어 = German.
T1-212.t: Pronounced [도길]: the batchim ㄱ links to the next vowel.

T1-213.x: Have you ever been to France?
T1-213.e: From French 'France'. The old Sino-Korean name 불란서 still pops up now and then.

T1-214.x: There are really a lot of people in Seoul.
T1-214.e: Native word that originally meant 'capital' — unlike most Korean place names, it has no hanja.

T1-216.x: My grandmother lives in the countryside.

T1-217.e: Literally 'old home'. Koreans head to their 고향 for 설날 and 추석.
T1-217.t: 고향이 어디예요? is a common get-to-know-you question; it can mean your home country too.

T1-218.x: I went to the mountains with friends on the weekend.
T1-218.e: Mountain names end in -산, like 남산. Hiking is a national pastime.

T1-219.x: I swim in the sea in summer.

T1-220.x: I walked along the river in the evening.
T1-220.e: River names end in -강: 한강 is the big river through Seoul.

T1-221.x: The traffic is really bad. (lit. The road is very blocked.)
T1-221.e: Also means 'way' or method. 길을 잃었어요 = I got lost.
T1-221.t: 길을 건너다 = to cross the street; 길을 묻다 = to ask for directions.

T1-222.x: There are lots of parks in my neighborhood.
T1-222.e: 동 (village) + native 네. City neighborhoods are named 'X동' in addresses.

T1-223.x: The kids are playing soccer on the field.
T1-223.e: 운동 (exercise) + 장 (ground). -장 = place, as in 수영장 (swimming pool).

T1-224.x: I looked around a museum on the weekend.
T1-224.t: Pronounced [방물관]: ㄱ before ㅁ becomes ㅇ. Romanized bangmulgwan.

T1-225.x: I live on the tenth floor of an apartment building.
T1-225.e: From English 'apartment', but it means a high-rise apartment complex — where most Koreans live.
T1-225.t: Small units are 원룸 or 빌라.

T1-226.x: That tall building is our company.

T1-228.x: I want to travel to many countries around the world.
T1-228.e: Both parts point to 'world'. 세계 지도 = world map.

T1-229.x: Let's meet in front of the school.
T1-229.e: 학교 앞 = in front of the school. 앞으로 = from now on.

T1-230.x: There is a small garden behind the house.
T1-230.t: Also used for time: 한 시간 뒤에 = an hour later (like 후에).

T1-231.x: There's a convenience store next to the bank.
T1-231.e: 옆집 = the house next door; 옆 사람 = the person beside you.

T1-232.x: There is a book on the desk.
T1-232.e: Opposite of 아래 and 밑. Heads-up: a different 위 means stomach.
T1-232.t: Korean puts the object first: 책상 위에 = 'desk top-at' → on the desk.

T1-233.t: 아래 and 밑 are often interchangeable; 밑 suggests directly underneath.

T1-234.x: The cat is under the bed.
T1-234.e: Directly underneath or the bottom: 책상 밑 = under the desk.

T1-235.x: There is a book inside the bag.
T1-235.t: Pattern: noun + 안에 = inside the noun. Don't confuse with the negative adverb 안 (not).

T1-236.t: Pronounced [바께] in 밖에: the ㄲ batchim carries over to the next syllable.

T1-237.x: The bank is between the post office and the hospital.
T1-237.e: Also means relationship: 사이가 좋다 = to get along well.
T1-237.t: Pattern: A와/하고 B 사이에 = between A and B. Often shortened to 새 in speech.

T1-238.x: There's a convenience store near my house.
T1-238.t: Pattern: noun + 근처에 = near the noun, e.g. 학교 근처에.

T1-239.t: Use 으로 for direction: 오른쪽으로 도세요 = turn right. Synonym: 오른편.

T1-240.x: The restroom is on the left.

T1-241.ex: 사진 가운데에 있는 사람이 제 동생이에요.
T1-241.x: The person in the middle of the photo is my younger sibling.
T1-241.e: Also means 'among': 우리 가운데 = among us.

T1-242.m: the other side, the opposite side (across)
T1-242.x: There's a café across the street.
T1-242.e: 건너다 (to cross) + 편 (side) — the side you'd cross over to.
T1-242.t: Common phrase: 길 건너편 = across the street.

T1-243.x: You can go this way to get to the station.
T1-243.e: Builds 오른쪽 (right) and 왼쪽 (left). Also means 'page'.
T1-243.t: Combines with 이/그/저/어느: 이쪽, 그쪽, 저쪽, 어느 쪽. 이쪽 also politely means 'this person'.

T1-245.t: 밥 means any meal: 밥 먹었어요? (Did you eat?) is a common greeting. For elders: 진지 드셨어요?

T1-246.x: I have bread and milk in the morning.
T1-246.e: From Portuguese 'pão' via Japanese 'pan' — not from English.

T1-247.x: I eat rice and soup together.
T1-247.e: Not the 국 'country' in 한국 — a different word. 국물 = broth.
T1-247.t: 국 is thin and brothy; 찌개 is thicker and saltier. Both are eaten with rice.

T1-248.x: This kimchi is a bit spicy.
T1-248.e: Probably from an old word meaning 'soaked vegetables'.

T1-250.e: 비빔 (mixing, from 비비다 to mix) + 밥 (rice) — 'mixed rice'.
T1-250.t: Pronounced [비빔빱]: 밥 becomes tense in this compound.

T1-251.x: I pack gimbap when I go on a picnic.
T1-251.e: 김 (dried seaweed) + 밥 (rice). Not the surname 김 — just a look-alike.

T1-252.x: I was hungry, so I made ramyeon.
T1-252.e: From Japanese 'ramen' — but in Korea it usually means instant noodles.
T1-252.t: You 'boil' ramyeon in Korean: 라면을 끓이다.

T1-253.x: I often eat cold noodles in summer.
T1-253.e: Literally 'cold noodles' — a classic summer dish.

T1-254.x: We eat rice cake soup on Lunar New Year's Day.
T1-254.e: Base of 떡볶이. 떡국 (rice cake soup) is eaten on New Year's Day.

T1-255.x: I ate tteokbokki with my friend.
T1-255.e: 떡 (rice cake) + 볶이 (from 볶다 to stir-fry). Same 볶 as 볶음밥 (fried rice).
T1-255.t: Pronounced [떡뽀끼]. Note the spelling: 볶 has a ㄲ batchim.

T1-256.e: Base of 소고기, 돼지고기, 닭고기, 불고기. 물고기 (water + meat) = fish.

T1-257.t: 쇠고기 is an equally standard spelling of the same word.

T1-258.x: I put pork in kimchi stew.

T1-259.e: 닭 (chicken) + 고기 (meat). Fried chicken is just 치킨.
T1-259.t: Pronounced [닥꼬기]: in 닭, only ㄱ is pronounced before a consonant.

T1-260.t: 생선 is fish as food; a live, swimming fish is 물고기.

T1-261.x: I eat two eggs every morning.
T1-261.t: 달걀 is the native synonym. 계 is usually pronounced [게].

T1-262.x: Eat lots of vegetables for your health.
T1-262.t: 야채 is very common in speech; 채소 is the more standard word.

T1-263.e: Probably from older 과실 (fruit) — its 과 likely the same 'fruit' as in 사과.

T1-264.e: Sino-Korean, but the parts don't add up — learn it whole.
T1-264.t: Homonym: 사과 (謝過) also means 'apology' — 사과하다 = to apologize.

T1-265.x: Korean pears are big and sweet.
T1-265.e: Same sound as 배 (belly) and 배 (boat). Korean pears are big, round and crisp.
T1-265.t: 배 also means 'stomach' and 'boat' — context tells you which.

T1-266.x: How much is a bunch of bananas?
T1-266.e: From English 'banana' — three even syllables: ba-na-na.

T1-267.x: The strawberries are very sweet and tasty.
T1-267.e: 딸기 우유 (strawberry milk) is a favorite Korean convenience-store drink.

T1-268.x: I bought grapes at the market.
T1-268.e: Sino-Korean, but the syllables have no separate meaning. 포도주 = wine ('grape alcohol').
T1-268.t: For wine, 와인 is also common.

T1-270.x: I eat a lot of tangerines in winter.
T1-270.t: Jeju Island is famous for 귤.

T1-271.x: You make cooked rice from raw rice.
T1-271.t: 쌀 is raw rice; once cooked it's 밥. Pronounce the tense ㅆ sharply.

T1-272.x: I boiled some potatoes and ate them.
T1-272.e: From an older Sino-Korean word for 'sweet tuber'. Sweet potato is now 고구마.

T1-274.e: Builds 물고기 (fish) and 물냉면 (cold noodles in broth).
T1-274.t: Restaurants serve water free, often self-service: 물은 셀프예요.

T1-275.x: The child drinks milk every day.

T1-276.x: Shall we have a cup of coffee?
T1-276.e: From English 'coffee'. Sounds like 'keopi' — Korean has no f sound.

T1-277.x: Have a cup of warm tea.
T1-277.t: 차 also means 'car' (車) — context makes it clear. Tea names: 녹차, 홍차, 보리차.

T1-278.t: Standard spelling is 주스, though you'll often see 쥬스 on signs.

T1-279.x: Let's have a beer after work.
T1-279.t: Pronounced [맥쭈]. 치맥 = chicken + beer, a popular combo.

T1-280.e: General word for any alcohol. 술집 = bar.
T1-280.t: With elders, hold your glass with two hands and turn your head slightly away to drink.

T1-282.x: I ordered a hamburger and a cola.
T1-282.e: From English 'cola'. Ask for 콜라 rather than 'Coke'.

T1-283.x: Do you put sugar in your coffee?

T1-284.x: I added a little salt to the soup.

T1-285.e: 맛있다 = delicious ('taste exists'); 맛없다 = not tasty.
T1-285.t: 맛이 is pronounced [마시]. 맛있다 is [마싣따] (also accepted: [마딛따]).

T1-286.x: Could I have some more side dishes, please?
T1-286.t: At Korean restaurants, 반찬 are usually free and refillable.

T1-287.e: 술 (spoonful) + 가락 (thin stick); ㄹ became ㄷ.
T1-287.t: Pronounced [숟까락]. Spelling trap: ㄷ in 숟가락 but ㅅ in 젓가락.

T1-288.e: 저 (Sino-Korean for chopsticks) + ㅅ + 가락 (thin stick), like 숟가락 and 손가락.
T1-288.t: Pronounced [저까락] or [젇까락]. Korean chopsticks are usually metal and flat.

T1-290.x: Please pour water into the cup.
T1-290.e: From English 'cup' — also used for glasses: 물 한 컵 = a glass of water.

T1-291.x: Please put the plates on the table.
T1-291.t: Pronounced [접씨]. Also a counter: 만두 한 접시 = one plate of dumplings.

T1-292.x: Could we have the menu here, please?
T1-292.t: 메뉴 can mean a dish itself; the physical menu card is 메뉴판.

T1-293.forms: 식사가 · 식사를 · 식사하다 (to have a meal)
T1-293.t: More polite than 밥: 식사하셨어요? = Have you eaten? Pronounced [식싸].

T1-294.e: 요리하다 = to cook; 한국 요리 = Korean cuisine.

T1-295.e: From English 'cake' — note the extra syllable: 'keikeu'.

T1-296.x: It's hot, so I want to eat ice cream.
T1-296.e: From English 'ice cream', said in five syllables: a-i-seu-keu-rim.

T1-297.t: 과자 covers packaged snacks — chips, crackers, cookies alike.

T1-298.e: 몸살 = achy, run-down feeling from fatigue — a very common complaint.
T1-298.t: 몸이 안 좋아요 = I'm not feeling well. 몸조심하세요 = Take care of yourself.

T1-299.x: I've had a headache since yesterday.
T1-299.t: 머리 often means hair: 머리를 잘랐어요 = I got a haircut. 머리가 좋다 = smart.

T1-300.e: Being told 얼굴이 작아요 (your face is small) is a compliment in Korea.
T1-300.t: 얼굴이 좋아 보여요 = You look well (healthy).

T1-301.x: That child has really big eyes.
T1-301.t: 눈 also means 'snow'; in careful speech 'snow' has a long vowel [눈ː].

T1-302.x: My nose is stuffed up because of a cold.

T1-303.e: Not related to 입다 (to wear) — just a look-alike.
T1-303.t: 입에 맞다 = to suit one's taste: 음식이 입에 맞아요?

T1-304.x: My ears hurt because of the music.

T1-305.x: I caught a cold, so my throat hurts.
T1-305.t: 목이 아파요 can mean a sore throat or a stiff neck.

T1-306.x: My shoulders hurt from using the computer too long.

T1-307.x: I fell and hurt my arm.
T1-307.e: Same sound as 팔 (eight) — a different word.
T1-307.t: Homonym: 팔 (八) is the Sino-Korean number eight.

T1-308.e: Base of 손가락 (finger) and 손목 (wrist, 'hand neck').
T1-308.t: Give and receive things with two hands when dealing with elders.

T1-309.x: I cut my finger on a knife.
T1-309.t: Pronounced [손까락]. Toes are 발가락 — literally 'foot fingers'.

T1-310.x: I skipped lunch, so I'm hungry.
T1-310.e: Also means pear and boat — context tells you which.
T1-310.t: 배가 고프다 = hungry, 배가 부르다 = full, 배가 아프다 = stomachache.

T1-311.x: My legs hurt because I walked a lot.
T1-311.t: 다리 also means 'bridge' — 한강 다리 = a bridge over the Han River.

T1-312.x: My feet hurt because my shoes are small.

T1-313.x: My lower back hurts because I sat for a long time.
T1-313.t: 허리 covers both the waist and the lower back: 허리가 아파요 usually means 'My back hurts.'

T1-314.x: My younger sibling has long hair.
T1-314.t: In everyday speech 머리 alone often means hair: 머리를 잘랐어요 = I got a haircut.

T1-315.x: My younger brother is very tall.
T1-315.e: Not to be confused with 키 'key' from English.
T1-315.t: Say 키가 커요 (tall) and 키가 작아요 (short) — not 길다/짧다.

T1-316.x: My grandmother got sick and went to the hospital.
T1-316.t: Don't confuse with 병 'bottle' (물 한 병). Common phrases: 병이 나다 (get sick), 병에 걸리다 (catch a disease).

T1-317.x: I've had a cold since yesterday, so my throat hurts.
T1-317.t: Use 감기에 걸리다 'to catch a cold' — note the particle 에.

T1-318.x: Please take the medicine after eating.
T1-318.t: Koreans 'eat' medicine: 약을 먹다 = to take medicine.

T1-319.ex: 아이가 열이 나서 학교에 못 갔어요.
T1-319.x: The child had a fever and couldn't go to school.
T1-319.t: 'To have a fever' is 열이 나다. Don't confuse with the native number 열 (ten).

T1-320.x: My older sister is a doctor who works at a hospital.
T1-320.t: When speaking to a doctor, call them 선생님 or 의사 선생님.

T1-322.x: I exercise every day for my health.
T1-322.t: 건강하세요! ('Stay healthy!') is a common warm goodbye or New Year wish.

T1-323.x: I bought new clothes at the department store on the weekend.
T1-323.e: 옷장 = wardrobe; 옷 가게 = clothing store. 옷을 입다 = put on clothes.
T1-323.t: Pronounced [옫]; with a vowel after it the ㅅ comes back: 옷이 [오시], 옷을 [오슬].

T1-324.e: 청바지 = jeans (literally 'blue pants'); 반바지 = shorts ('half pants').

T1-325.x: My older sister is wearing a red skirt.
T1-325.e: Also the name of the long, full skirt worn with a hanbok.

T1-326.ex: 회사에 갈 때 하얀 셔츠를 입어요.
T1-326.x: I wear a white shirt when I go to work.
T1-326.e: From English 'shirt'. Usually means a button-up; a tee is 티셔츠.

T1-327.x: In summer I usually wear T-shirts.
T1-327.e: From English 'T-shirt', often shortened to 티. 반팔 티 = short-sleeve tee.

T1-328.ex: 친구 결혼식에 파란 원피스를 입고 갔어요.
T1-328.x: I wore a blue dress to my friend's wedding.
T1-328.t: Konglish: 원피스 means a woman's dress, not a one-piece swimsuit.

T1-329.x: It was cold, so I wore a thick coat.
T1-329.e: From English 'coat'. 코트 can also mean a sports court, like 테니스 코트.

T1-330.x: It was cold, so I put on thick socks.
T1-330.t: Socks and shoes use 신다, not 입다: 양말을 신어요.

T1-331.x: In Korean homes you take off your shoes.
T1-331.e: 신 (shoe) + 발 (foot). 신다 is also for socks.
T1-331.t: Put shoes on with 신다 and take them off with 벗다.

T1-332.x: I wore new dress shoes on the day of the interview.
T1-332.e: Probably from Japanese kutsu (shoes). Means formal leather shoes; sneakers are 운동화.

T1-333.x: I put on sneakers and walked in the park.

T1-334.x: The sun was strong, so I wore a hat.
T1-334.e: 모 (hat) + 자, a common noun ending.
T1-334.t: Hats and glasses use 쓰다: 모자를 쓰다, 안경을 쓰다.

T1-335.x: There are books and a wallet in my bag.
T1-335.e: From Japanese kaban (bag). Covers any bag: backpack, purse, briefcase.

T1-336.ex: 저는 책을 읽을 때 안경을 써요.
T1-336.x: I wear glasses when I read books.
T1-336.t: Glasses are 'worn' with 쓰다: 안경을 써요. Sunglasses are 선글라스.

T1-337.x: I gave my father a watch for his birthday.
T1-337.t: Pronounced [시게] in everyday speech. A watch is 'worn' with 차다: 시계를 차다.

T1-338.x: It's raining. Take an umbrella with you.
T1-338.t: You 'wear' an umbrella with 쓰다: 우산을 쓰다 = to hold up an umbrella.

T1-339.x: I got a wallet as a birthday present.

T1-340.x: I don't have much money this month.
T1-340.e: 용돈 = pocket money; 세뱃돈 = cash kids get for bowing to elders at Lunar New Year.
T1-340.t: Useful pairs: 돈을 벌다 (earn money), 돈을 쓰다 (spend money), 돈을 내다 (pay).

T1-341.e: Spelled with ㅄ. 밥값 = meal cost.
T1-341.t: Pronounced [갑]; before a vowel the ㅅ returns as ㅆ: 값이 [갑씨], 값을 [갑쓸].

T1-342.x: How much do these sneakers cost?
T1-342.t: 가격 is a bit more formal than native 값; you'll see it on signs and price tags.

T1-343.x: This store has a lot of good items.

T1-344.x: I bought flowers as a birthday present for my friend.
T1-344.e: Literally 'offered thing'. Here 물 means 'thing', not 'water'.

T1-345.t: Use 로: 카드로 계산하다 / 카드로 내다 = pay by card.

T1-346.x: At the market it's better to pay in cash.

T1-347.x: Could I have the receipt, please?
T1-347.t: Cashiers often ask 영수증 드릴까요? — 'Would you like the receipt?'

T1-348.x: My father goes to work by car.
T1-348.t: Homonym: 차 also means tea (茶). Context tells you which: 차를 마셔요 vs 차를 타요.

T1-349.x: There are lots of cars on the road, so traffic is jammed.

T1-350.ex: 저는 매일 버스를 타고 학교에 가요.
T1-350.x: I take the bus to school every day.
T1-350.e: From English 'bus'. Sounds like 'beoseu' — Korean adds a vowel after the final s.
T1-350.t: Transport takes 를/을 with 타다: 버스를 타요 (take the bus); get off is 버스에서 내려요.

T1-351.x: The subway is very convenient in Seoul.
T1-351.e: Literally 'underground iron (rail)'. 지하 alone means basement or underground.

T1-352.x: It takes about three hours to Busan by train.
T1-352.e: Literally 'steam vehicle', from the steam-engine era.

T1-353.x: I was late, so I took a taxi.
T1-353.e: From English 'taxi'. 택시를 타다 = take a taxi.
T1-353.t: Pronounced [택씨]: ㅅ after a ㄱ batchim becomes tense ㅆ.

T1-354.x: Tomorrow I'm flying to Jeju Island.

T1-355.x: We took a boat to the island.
T1-355.t: 배 also means 'belly' and 'pear'. 배가 아파요 = my stomach hurts; 배를 타요 = I take a boat.

T1-356.x: On weekends I ride my bike by the river.

T1-357.e: 기차표 = train ticket; 비행기표 = plane ticket.
T1-357.t: Count tickets with 장: 표 한 장, 표 두 장.

T1-358.e: Literally 'move and turn'. 운전하다 = to drive.

T1-359.x: Transportation is very convenient in this neighborhood.
T1-359.e: Literally 'crossing and passing'. 교통카드 = transit card.

T1-360.x: Cross when the traffic light turns green.

T1-361.x: If you cross this bridge, there's a market.
T1-361.t: 다리 also means 'leg'. 다리가 아파요 = my legs hurt; 다리를 건너요 = I cross the bridge.

T1-362.x: I study Korean at the library.
T1-362.e: Sino-Korean, but the parts don't add up to 'study' — just learn it whole. 공부하다 = to study.
T1-362.t: Both 한국어를 공부해요 and 한국어 공부를 해요 are natural.

T1-363.x: I'm busy today because I have a lot of homework.
T1-363.e: Literally 'overnight task' — work you take home.
T1-363.t: Pronounced [숙쩨]: ㅈ after a ㄱ batchim becomes tense ㅉ.

T1-364.x: I have a Korean exam next week.
T1-364.t: 'Take an exam' is 시험을 보다 (literally 'see an exam').

T1-365.x: What time does today's class end?
T1-365.t: 'Take a class' is 수업을 듣다 (literally 'listen to a class').

T1-366.x: I read a book before going to sleep.
T1-366.t: Count books with 권: 책 한 권, 책 두 권.

T1-367.x: I write new words in my notebook.
T1-367.t: A book with blank pages to write in.

T1-368.t: Count pencils and pens with 자루: 연필 한 자루 (or casually 연필 하나).

T1-369.x: Please write your name with a black pen.
T1-369.t: Koreans say 볼펜 for an ordinary pen; 펜 is also used.

T1-370.x: Please write your phone number on the paper.
T1-370.e: 종이컵 = paper cup; 종이접기 = origami (literally 'paper folding').
T1-370.t: Count sheets with 장: 종이 한 장.

T1-371.x: I look up words I don't know in the dictionary.
T1-371.e: Literally 'words reference book'. 영한사전 = English-Korean dictionary.
T1-371.t: Homonym: 사전 (事前) also means 'beforehand', as in 사전 예약.

T1-372.x: There is a computer on the desk.
T1-372.t: Pronounced [책쌍]: ㅅ after a ㄱ batchim becomes tense ㅆ.

T1-373.x: Please sit in this chair here.
T1-373.e: 의 (chair) + 자, a common noun ending.

T1-374.t: 문제없어요! = 'No problem!' For a question you ask someone, use 질문 instead.

T1-376.t: Use 에 for what you answer: 질문에 대답하다.

T1-377.x: Korean is fun but a little difficult.
T1-377.e: 한국 (Korea) + 어 (language). Add -어 to a country for its language: 중국어, 일본어.
T1-377.t: Pronounced [한구거]. 한국말 is the more conversational word for the same thing.

T1-378.ex: 저는 영어하고 한국어를 할 수 있어요.
T1-378.x: I can speak English and Korean.

T1-379.x: Learning a foreign language is fun.

T1-380.x: What that person said is right.
T1-380.e: 말하다 = to speak. Say it longer for 'words'.
T1-380.t: Homonym: 말 also means 'horse'. For elders' words use 말씀: 선생님 말씀.

T1-381.x: I wrote a short text in Korean.
T1-381.e: 글씨 = handwriting; 글자 = letter, character; 한글 = Korean alphabet.
T1-381.t: 말 is spoken language; 글 is written language.

T1-382.ex: 매일 새 단어를 열 개씩 외워요.
T1-382.x: I memorize ten new words every day.
T1-382.e: Literally 'single word'. 단어를 외우다 = memorize words.

T1-383.x: Try making a sentence with this word.

T1-384.e: Super useful phrase: 이 단어 뜻이 뭐예요? = What does this word mean?
T1-384.t: Pronounced [뜯]; before a vowel the ㅅ sound returns: 뜻이 [뜨시].

T1-385.e: 글 = writing; 한 probably 'great' or 'Korean'. Created by King Sejong in 1443; name coined about 1912.
T1-385.t: 한글 is the writing system, not the language — the language is 한국어.

T1-386.x: I have a meeting at two in the afternoon.

T1-387.x: There's a lot of work at the company these days.
T1-387.t: Not to be confused with Sino-Korean 일 'one' (一) or 'day' (日).

T1-388.x: What do you do for a living?
T1-388.t: Pronounced [지겁]. More polite question: 무슨 일을 하세요?

T1-389.x: My older brother is an office worker.

T1-390.x: I got lost, so I asked a police officer.
T1-390.e: 경찰서 = police station; 경찰관 = police officer.

T1-391.x: My older brother is a hotel chef.

T1-392.ex: 저는 그 가수의 노래를 정말 좋아해요.
T1-392.x: I really like that singer's songs.
T1-392.e: Literally 'song hand' — 수 marks a skilled person.

T1-393.x: That actor is very famous in Korea.
T1-393.t: Don't confuse with the verb 배우다 (to learn): 배워요 means 'I learn', not 'actor'.

T1-394.ex: 제 동생은 서울에 있는 대학교에 다녀요.
T1-394.x: My younger sibling goes to a university in Seoul.
T1-394.t: Pronounced [대학꾜]. In speech 대학 alone is also common: 대학에 가요.

T1-395.x: I'm a university student. I study Korean.
T1-395.t: Pronounced [대학쌩]: ㅅ after a ㄱ batchim becomes tense ㅆ.

T1-396.t: Pronounced [조럽]. The school takes 을/를: 학교를 졸업하다 (not 학교에서).

T1-397.ex: 우리 반에는 학생이 열다섯 명 있어요.
T1-397.x: There are fifteen students in our class.
T1-397.e: Two words: 'class' (우리 반 = our class) and 'half'.
T1-397.t: 'Half' is common with time: 세 시 반 = 3:30. For 'class' meaning a lesson, use 수업 instead.

T1-398.x: Please open your textbook to page 20.

T1-399.x: It's cold. Please close the door.
T1-399.t: Common pair: 문을 열다 (open the door) · 문을 닫다 (close the door; also 'a shop closes').

T1-400.x: If it's hot, open the window.

T1-401.x: There is a big bed in my room.

T1-402.x: My father is watching TV on the sofa.
T1-402.t: Korean has no f sound, so English f becomes ㅍ: sofa → 소파, coffee → 커피.

T1-403.x: The milk is in the fridge.

T1-404.x: I eat dinner and watch TV.
T1-404.e: From English 'television'; usually shortened to 티비 (TV).
T1-404.t: In speech people often say 티브이 (TV). 'Watch TV' = 텔레비전을 보다.

T1-405.x: I do my homework on the computer.

T1-406.t: Often sounds like [저놔] in natural speech. 'Answer the phone' = 전화를 받다.

T1-407.x: I left my phone at home.
T1-407.t: 핸드폰 and 휴대폰 are both everyday words for a mobile phone; 폰 alone is casual.

T1-408.t: Phone numbers use Sino-Korean digits; 0 is 공: 010 = 공일공.

T1-409.x: May I take a photo here?

T1-410.x: I took a lot of pictures with my new camera.

T1-411.x: I look in the mirror every morning.
T1-411.t: 'Look in the mirror' = 거울을 보다 (object particle, no 'in').

T1-412.e: 열다 (to open) + 쇠 (iron) — literally 'opening metal'. Compare 자물쇠 (lock).

T1-413.x: It was cold, so I slept under a blanket.
T1-413.e: Slang 이불킥 ('blanket kick') = cringing in bed over an embarrassing memory.
T1-413.t: 'Cover oneself with a blanket' = 이불을 덮다.

T1-414.x: Turn off the light when you leave the room.
T1-414.e: Both fire and light. 불고기 = 'fire meat'.
T1-414.t: 불을 켜다 = turn on the light; 불을 끄다 = turn off. 불이 났어요! = There's a fire!

T1-415.ex: 너무 더워요. 에어컨 좀 켜 주세요.
T1-415.x: It's too hot. Please turn on the air conditioner.
T1-415.e: From English 'air con(ditioner)' — Koreans clip it; Americans would say AC.

T1-416.x: I put the clothes in the washing machine.

T1-417.x: I cleaned my room on the weekend.

T1-418.x: I have to do the laundry today.

T1-419.x: Please throw the trash away over there.
T1-419.e: Probably from 쓸다 (to sweep). 쓰레기통 = trash can.

T1-420.x: There's no toilet paper in the bathroom.

T1-421.ex: 밥 먹기 전에 비누로 손을 씻으세요.
T1-421.x: Wash your hands with soap before eating.

T1-422.x: I put a toothbrush in my travel bag.

T1-423.x: Please give me one more towel.

T1-424.e: 상 (box) + 자, a noun ending — so just 'box'.

T1-425.x: I wrote a letter to my parents.
T1-425.e: Sino-Korean, but the parts don't add up; 지 = paper, as in 휴지 (tissue).
T1-425.t: 편지 is a letter you send, not a letter of the alphabet (글자).

T1-426.x: Please write your name and address here.

T1-427.x: I sent an email to my teacher.

T1-428.x: The weather is really nice today.
T1-428.e: Built on 날 (day): the day's condition. 날씨가 좋아요 = the weather's nice.
T1-428.t: Ask about weather with 날씨가 어때요? (How's the weather?)

T1-429.x: It's raining outside. Do you have an umbrella?
T1-429.t: 'It's raining' = 비가 와요 or 비가 내려요.

T1-430.e: Snow is said with a longer vowel.
T1-430.t: 눈 also means 'eye'. Context tells them apart: 눈이 와요 (it snows) vs 눈이 아파요 (my eyes hurt).

T1-431.e: Also means 'a wish' (from 바라다, to hope). 바람을 피우다 = to cheat on a partner.

T1-432.x: There isn't a single cloud in the sky.

T1-433.x: The autumn sky is really blue.

T1-434.x: In the countryside you can see the stars well at night.
T1-434.e: 별 다섯 개 = five stars (a rating). Unrelated to 별로 (not really).

T1-435.x: In spring, lots of flowers bloom in the park.
T1-435.e: 꽃집 = flower shop; 꽃미남 = 'flower boy', a pretty-faced guy.
T1-435.t: Pronounced [꼳] alone, but the ㅊ returns before a vowel: 꽃이 [꼬치], 꽃을 [꼬츨].

T1-436.ex: 우리 집 앞에 큰 나무가 있어요.
T1-436.x: There's a big tree in front of our house.
T1-436.e: Means tree and wood. 소나무 = pine tree; 나뭇잎 = leaf.

T1-438.ex: 저는 집에서 개를 한 마리 키워요.
T1-438.x: I have a dog at home.
T1-438.t: Don't mix up with the counter 개 (items): 사과 두 개. Count animals with 마리: 개 두 마리.

T1-439.x: The cat is sleeping on the sofa.

T1-440.x: I can hear birds singing in the morning.
T1-440.t: 새 before a noun means 'new': 새 옷 (new clothes). As a noun on its own it means 'bird'.

T1-441.x: There are lots of fish in the river.
T1-441.t: 물고기 is a live fish; fish you eat is usually 생선. Pronounced [물꼬기].

T1-442.x: There's a big rock on the road. Be careful.
T1-442.t: 돌 also means a baby's first birthday (돌잔치 = first-birthday party).

T1-443.e: Literally 'interest-taste'. 취미가 뭐예요? = What's your hobby?
T1-443.t: Answer with 제 취미는 … 이에요/예요, or -는 것: 제 취미는 노래하는 거예요.

T1-445.x: I play soccer with my friends on weekends.
T1-445.t: Ball sports use 하다: 축구를 하다 (play soccer). Pronounced [축꾸].

T1-447.x: I played basketball in the school gym.

T1-448.x: In summer I swim in the sea.

T1-449.x: I play tennis with my older sister every Saturday.
T1-449.t: Racket and hitting sports use 치다: 테니스를 치다, 탁구를 치다, 골프를 치다.

T1-450.x: My father goes hiking every weekend.
T1-450.e: Literally 'climbing a mountain' — a hugely popular weekend hobby in Korea.
T1-450.t: Both 등산을 하다 and 등산을 가다 (go hiking) are common.

T1-451.x: I'm going on a trip to Jeju Island during vacation.
T1-451.t: 'Go on a trip' = 여행(을) 가다. 여행사 = travel agency.

T1-453.x: I listen to music when I study.
T1-453.t: Pronounced [으막]. 'Listen to music' = 음악을 듣다 → 들어요.

T1-454.x: Let's sing at a karaoke room.
T1-454.e: Probably from 놀다 (to play). 노래방 = karaoke room.
T1-454.t: 'Sing a song' = 노래(를) 하다 or 노래를 부르다.

T1-455.t: 'To dance' = 춤을 추다 (추 + 어요 → 춰요), not 춤하다.

T1-456.x: My younger sibling drew a picture of a cat.
T1-456.t: 'Draw a picture' = 그림을 그리다. A photo is 사진, not 그림.

T1-457.x: My younger sibling plays computer games every day.
T1-457.e: From English 'game'. A PC방 ('PC room') is a gaming café.

T1-458.t: 독서 is a bit formal; in everyday speech people say 책을 읽어요. Pronounced [독써].

T1-459.forms: 산책이 · 산책을 · 산책하다 (to take a walk)
T1-459.x: I went out for a walk with my dog.
T1-459.e: Sino-Korean, but this 책 isn't 'book' — just learn it whole. 산책하다 = take a walk.

T1-460.x: I learned piano when I was a child.
T1-460.t: 'Play the piano' = 피아노를 치다 (치다 = hit, strike).

T1-461.x: My older brother plays the guitar very well.
T1-461.e: From English 'guitar'. Don't mix up with 기타 meaning 'etc., other'.
T1-461.t: Homonym: Sino-Korean 기타 (其他) means 'others, etc.' 'Play guitar' = 기타를 치다.

T1-462.ex: 다음 주에 좋아하는 가수 콘서트에 가요.
T1-462.x: Next week I'm going to my favorite singer's concert.

T1-463.x: These days I often watch Korean dramas.
T1-463.t: In Korean, 드라마 means any TV series, including comedies and romances.

T1-464.x: My father watches the news every morning.

T1-465.t: 'Online / via the internet' = 인터넷으로. Pronounced [인터넫]; before 이/을: [인터네시], [인터네슬].

T1-466.x: I decided to go shopping with a friend this weekend.
T1-466.e: From English 'shopping'. 쇼핑하다 = to go shopping.

T1-467.x: There's a friend's birthday party on Saturday.

T1-468.t: 것 needs a word before it: 제 것 (mine), 먹을 것 (something to eat). In speech it shortens to 거: 제 거예요.

T1-469.e: 사랑해 is heard in nearly every K-drama.
T1-469.t: Add 하다 to make the verb: 사랑하다 'to love'. 사랑해요 = 'I love you.'

T1-470.e: 생각하다 = to think; 생각나다 = to come to mind (lit. 'a thought comes out').
T1-470.t: 생각이 나다 can also mean 'to remember'. 생각해요 = 'I think.'

T1-471.x: I talked with my friend for a long time.
T1-471.t: In speech it's often shortened to 얘기: 얘기해요.

T1-472.x: There's a strange sound coming from outside.
T1-472.e: 목소리 = voice (목 throat + 소리 sound); 소리 지르다 = to shout.

T1-473.x: What's the reason you were late?
T1-473.e: Literally 'reason + cause' — 왜? (why?) is answered with an 이유.

T1-474.x: Do you have any plans this weekend?
T1-474.t: Usually pronounced [게획] or [게훽]: 계 is commonly said like 게.

T1-475.x: I have plans with a friend this evening.
T1-475.t: 약속 covers both 'promise' and 'plans to meet someone'. Pronounced [약쏙].

T1-476.x: Please contact me when you arrive.
T1-476.t: Pronounced [열락]: ㄴ before ㄹ becomes ㄹ.

T1-478.x: This bread has a pretty shape.
T1-478.e: Literally 'pattern + shape'. 무슨 모양? = what shape?

T1-479.e: Add -색 to make color words: 빨간색 = red.

T1-480.x: These clothes are a pretty color.
T1-480.t: 색깔 and 색 mean the same; 색깔 is more casual and stands alone, while 색 forms compounds like 빨간색.

T1-481.x: This shop has many kinds of bread.
T1-481.e: Literally 'kind + type'. 무슨 종류? = what kind?
T1-481.t: Pronounced [종뉴]: ㄹ after ㅇ becomes ㄴ.

T1-482.x: I'm in a really good mood today.
T1-482.t: 기분이 좋아요 = I feel good; 기분이 나빠요 = I'm upset / in a bad mood.

T1-483.x: That person has a warm heart.
T1-483.e: The emotional heart (the organ is 심장). 마음에 들다 is lit. 'enter the heart'.
T1-483.t: 마음에 들다 = 'to like, to be to one's liking': 이 가방이 마음에 들어요.

T1-484.x: My dream is to become a teacher.
T1-484.t: You 'dream a dream': 꿈을 꾸다. 어젯밤에 이상한 꿈을 꿨어요.

T1-485.e: 자리 있어요? = Is this seat taken? Also means a position or job opening.

T1-486.e: From 자다 (to sleep); 낮잠 = nap (낮 daytime).
T1-486.t: 잠을 자다 = to sleep; 잠이 오다 = to get sleepy; 잠이 안 와요 = I can't fall asleep.

T1-487.x: I greeted my teacher in the morning.
T1-487.e: 인사하다 = to greet or bow. Literally 'people matters' — it also means HR (personnel).

T1-488.x: Please show your passport at the airport.
T1-488.t: Pronounced [여꿘] with a tense ㄲ sound.

T1-489.x: I came to Korea for the first time.
T1-489.e: 처음 뵙겠습니다 = 'Nice to meet you' (lit. 'I'm seeing you for the first time').
T1-489.t: Also used as an adverb: 처음 왔어요.

T1-490.x: Today is the last day of class.
T1-490.e: Opposite of 처음 (first). 마지막 날 = the last day.

T1-491.x: I'm going to the sea with a friend this weekend.
T1-491.t: Destination takes 에: 학교에 가요. 안녕히 가세요 = goodbye (to someone leaving).

T1-492.t: Rain and snow 'come' in Korean: 비가 와요 = it's raining, 눈이 와요 = it's snowing.

T1-493.x: I had bread and milk in the morning.
T1-493.e: 먹다 → 먹이 (animal feed), 먹방 (mukbang = eating broadcast); 약을 먹다 = take medicine.
T1-493.t: For elders use 드시다 or 잡수시다: 많이 드세요 = 'Please eat a lot.'

T1-494.e: Used for drinks: 물/커피/술을 마시다. Soup and medicine usually take 먹다.
T1-494.t: 마시 + 어요 contracts to 마셔요. For elders, 드시다 is used for drinking too.

T1-495.x: I usually go to bed at eleven.
T1-495.t: 안녕히 주무세요 = 'Good night' to elders; to friends: 잘 자.

T1-496.m: to get up, to wake up; to stand up; to happen
T1-496.x: I get up at seven every day.
T1-496.e: 일다 (rise) + 나다 (come out) — 'rise up': wake up, stand up, or happen.
T1-496.t: Pronounced [이러나다]: the ㄹ batchim links to the next vowel.

T1-497.m: to see, to look at, to watch; to take (an exam)
T1-497.x: I watched a movie in the evening.
T1-497.t: After a verb, -아/어 보다 means 'try doing': 먹어 보세요 = try eating it. 시험을 보다 = take a test.

T1-498.forms: 들어요 · 들었어요 · 들을 거예요 · 들으세요 (ㄷ irregular)
T1-498.m: to listen, to hear; to take (a class)
T1-498.x: I listen to Korean music every day.
T1-498.e: 수업을 듣다 = to take a class.
T1-498.t: ㄷ irregular: ㄷ turns into ㄹ before a vowel — 듣다 → 들어요.

T1-499.m: to speak, to say, to tell
T1-499.e: 말 (words, speech) + 하다 (do). Careful: 말 also means 'horse'.
T1-499.t: Pronounced [말하다]; the ㅎ is kept in standard pronunciation (fast speech may weaken it). Honorific: 말씀하시다.

T1-500.x: I read the newspaper every morning.
T1-500.t: Pronounced [익따], but 읽어요 is [일거요] — the ㄹ comes back before a vowel.

T1-501.forms: 써요 · 썼어요 · 쓸 거예요 · 쓰세요 (ㅡ drops)
T1-501.x: I wrote a letter to my friend.
T1-501.t: 쓰다 also means 'to use', 'to wear (a hat/glasses)' and 'to be bitter' — context tells you which.

T1-502.forms: 써요 · 썼어요 · 쓸 거예요 · 쓰세요 (ㅡ drops)
T1-502.t: 돈을 쓰다 = to spend money. 사용하다 is a more formal synonym.

T1-503.forms: 써요 · 썼어요 · 쓸 거예요 · 쓰세요 (ㅡ drops)
T1-503.m: to wear, to put on (hat, glasses, mask); to hold up (umbrella)
T1-503.x: It was raining outside, so I used an umbrella.
T1-503.e: For the head and face: 모자/안경/마스크를 쓰다; 우산을 쓰다 = hold an umbrella.
T1-503.t: Korean has different 'wear' verbs: 입다 clothes, 신다 shoes/socks, 쓰다 hats/glasses/masks.

T1-504.e: Opposite of 가르치다 (teach). The noun 배우 (actor) is an unrelated word.

T1-505.x: My mother teaches English at school.
T1-505.t: Don't confuse with 가리키다 'to point at' — native speakers mix them up too.

T1-506.x: I study together with my friend at the library.
T1-506.e: 공부 (study) + 하다 (do). Sino-Korean, but the parts don't add up — learn 공부 whole.

T1-507.e: Native 일 (work) + 하다 (do). Different from 일 'day' and 일 'one'.
T1-507.t: Pronounced [일하다] (the ㅎ is kept in standard pronunciation). Place of work takes 에서: 회사에서 일해요.

T1-508.x: Let's meet in front of the school tomorrow.
T1-508.e: 만나서 반가워요 = Nice to meet you (lit. 'glad because we met').
T1-508.t: The person takes 을/를 or 하고: 친구를 만나요 / 친구하고 만나요.

T1-509.x: I bought fruit at the market.
T1-509.e: Opposite of 팔다 (sell). 사 줄게 = 'I'll treat you' — common when buying a friend a meal.
T1-509.t: 사다 'buy' and 살다 'live' share forms like 사세요 — context tells them apart.

T1-510.forms: 팔아요 · 팔았어요 · 팔 거예요 · 파세요 (ㄹ drops)
T1-510.x: Do they sell milk at this store?
T1-510.e: Opposite of 사다 (buy). 팔 also means 'arm' and 'eight'.
T1-510.t: ㄹ drops before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ: 파세요, 파는 사람 (seller).

T1-511.x: I gave my younger sibling a present.
T1-511.t: 주세요 = 'please give me'; after a verb, -아/어 주세요 = 'please do it for me': 도와주세요.

T1-512.m: to receive, to get; to answer (a phone)
T1-512.x: I got flowers for my birthday.
T1-512.t: 전화를 받다 = to answer the phone. Pronounced [받따].

T1-513.t: Pronounced [안따]; 앉아요 is [안자요] — the ㅈ reappears before a vowel.

T1-514.ex: 버스 정류장 앞에 사람들이 서 있어요.
T1-514.x: People are standing in front of the bus stop.
T1-514.e: 일어서다 = to stand up. For buses and cars it means 'to stop'.
T1-514.t: Use 서 있다 for the state 'be standing'.

T1-515.forms: 걸어요 · 걸었어요 · 걸을 거예요 · 걸으세요 (ㄷ irregular)
T1-515.x: I walk in the park every day.
T1-515.t: ㄷ irregular: 걷다 → 걸어요. Don't confuse with regular 걸다 'to hang', which also gives 걸어요.

T1-516.x: I run in the park every morning.
T1-516.t: Pronounced [달리다]. In everyday speech 뛰다 is very common for 'run'.

T1-517.forms: 놀아요 · 놀았어요 · 놀 거예요 · 노세요 (ㄹ drops)
T1-517.m: to play, to hang out; to be off (work)
T1-517.x: I hung out at my friend's house on the weekend.
T1-517.e: 놀이 = play, game; 놀이공원 = amusement park. 놀러 오세요 = come hang out.
T1-517.t: 놀다 is not for sports or instruments: use 하다 (축구를 하다) or 치다 (피아노를 치다).

T1-518.m: to rest, to take a break; to be closed (shop)
T1-518.x: On weekends I rest at home.
T1-518.e: 쉬는 시간 = break time. Don't confuse with 쉽다 (easy).
T1-518.t: 오늘 가게가 쉬어요 = the shop is closed today.

T1-519.forms: 살아요 · 살았어요 · 살 거예요 · 사세요 (ㄹ drops)
T1-519.e: 삶 (life) comes from 살다. 서울에 살아요 = I live in Seoul.
T1-519.t: Both 서울에서 살아요 and 서울에 살아요 are correct. 어디 사세요? = Where do you live?

T1-520.forms: 있어요 · 있었어요 · 있을 거예요 · 있는 (+noun) · honorific: 계세요 (be somewhere), 있으세요 (have)
T1-520.m: to be (somewhere), to exist; to have
T1-520.e: 맛있다 = tasty (lit. 'flavor exists'); 재미있다 = fun. Opposite: 없다.
T1-520.t: Possession uses 이/가: 시간이 있어요 = I have time. Modifier is 있는, not 있은.
rel: to not exist, to not have

T1-521.m: to not be (somewhere), to not exist; to not have

T1-522.forms: 이에요 (after consonant) / 예요 (after vowel) · 이었어요/였어요 · 일 거예요 · 이세요/세요
T1-522.t: 이다 attaches directly to the noun: 학생이에요, 의사예요. Formal: 학생입니다.

T1-523.e: Negative of 이다: 학생이 아니에요 = I'm not a student. 아니요 = no.
T1-523.t: The noun takes 이/가: 학생이 아니에요. 아니에요 alone also means 'Not at all / You're welcome.'

T1-524.m: to do; to make; to say
T1-524.x: What are you doing this evening?
T1-524.e: Turns nouns into verbs: 공부하다 (study), 운동하다 (exercise), 사랑하다 (love).

T1-525.m: to become; to be done, to work out; to be OK
T1-525.x: I want to become a doctor.
T1-525.e: 의사가 되다 = become a doctor; 돼요 = it's OK; 안 돼요 = no, not allowed.
T1-525.t: The result takes 이/가: 가수가 되다. Spell 돼요 (되어요), not 되요. -아/어도 돼요 = 'may I…'.

T1-526.forms: 알아요 · 알았어요 · 알 거예요 · 아세요 (ㄹ drops)
T1-526.x: Do you know that person's phone number?
T1-526.t: 알겠어요 / 알겠습니다 = 'Got it, understood.' 알았어요 is also used this way.

T1-527.forms: 몰라요 · 몰랐어요 · 모를 거예요 · 모르세요 (르 irregular)
T1-527.t: 르 irregular: 르 + 아요 → ㄹ라요, so 모르다 → 몰라요. Use 모르다 instead of 안 알다.

T1-528.e: 좋다 (good) + -아하다 (show a feeling). 좋아요 = it's good; 좋아해요 = I like it.
T1-528.t: 좋아하다 takes 을/를 (음식을 좋아해요); 좋다 takes 이/가 (음식이 좋아요). Pronounced [조아하다].

T1-529.x: My younger sibling doesn't like vegetables.
T1-529.e: 싫다 (unpleasant) + -어하다. 싫어요! = No, I don't want to!
T1-529.t: Pronounced [시러하다]: ㅎ in ㅀ is silent before a vowel.

T1-530.e: 사랑 (love) + 하다 (do). 사랑해요 = I love you.

T1-531.x: I waited for the bus for thirty minutes.
T1-531.e: 잠깐만 기다리세요 = Please wait a moment.
T1-531.t: The person or thing waited for takes 을/를: 버스를 기다려요 = I'm waiting for the bus.

T1-532.forms: 불러요 · 불렀어요 · 부를 거예요 · 부르세요 (르 irregular)
T1-532.m: to call (out); to sing; to be full (stomach, as 배가 부르다)
T1-532.x: I sang songs at the karaoke room.
T1-532.t: 노래를 부르다 = to sing a song; 배가 불러요 = I'm full.

T1-533.t: The person called takes 에게/한테: 엄마한테 전화해요. Often pronounced [저놔하다].

T1-534.x: I work out at the gym every evening.

T1-535.e: 요리 (cooking, cuisine) + 하다 (do). 한국 요리 = Korean food.

T1-536.x: I cleaned my room on Saturday.

T1-537.x: I wash fruit well before eating it.
T1-537.t: 씻다 is for body parts, dishes, food; for clothes use 빨다 / 빨래하다. Pronounced [씯따].

T1-538.x: I took a shower after working out.

T1-539.x: It's cold today, so I wore a coat.
T1-539.t: 입다 is for clothes worn on the body; shoes/socks use 신다, hats/glasses use 쓰다. Regular verb (not ㅂ irregular).

T1-540.x: Please take off your shoes here.
T1-540.e: 신발 벗으세요 = take off your shoes (at Korean homes).
T1-540.t: One verb for taking off everything — clothes, shoes, hats, glasses.

T1-541.m: to wear, to put on (shoes, socks)
T1-541.x: I put on sneakers and went out.
T1-541.e: Related to 신 (shoes), as in 신발. Used for shoes and socks.
T1-541.t: Pronounced [신따]: the ending tenses after ㄴ in verb stems.

T1-542.m: to ride, to take (a vehicle), to get on
T1-542.x: I take the subway to work.
T1-542.t: The vehicle takes 을/를: 버스를 타요. Also 자전거를 타다 'ride a bike'.

T1-543.m: to get off (a vehicle); to fall (rain, snow); to go down
T1-543.x: I get off at the next station.
T1-543.e: Opposite of 타다 (get on). 비가 내리다 = rain falls.
T1-543.t: The vehicle takes 에서: 버스에서 내려요.

T1-544.x: Transfer to Line 2 at City Hall Station.
T1-544.e: 갈다 (change) + 타다 (ride) — 'switch rides.' You'll hear it in Seoul subway announcements.
T1-544.t: The new line/vehicle takes (으)로: 버스로 갈아타요.

T1-545.m: to go in, to enter; to go back (home)
T1-545.x: It's cold, so let's go inside.
T1-545.e: 들다 (enter) + 가다 (go). Opposite: 나가다; 들어오다 = come in.
T1-545.t: 들어가세요 is also a polite goodbye: 'Get home safely.'

T1-546.ex: 저는 아침 여덟 시에 집에서 나가요.
T1-546.x: I leave the house at eight in the morning.
T1-546.t: 나가다 = go out (away from the speaker); 나오다 = come out (toward the speaker).

T1-547.m: to come in, to enter; to come home
T1-547.x: It's cold, so come inside quickly.
T1-547.e: 들다 (enter) + 오다 (come); compare 들어가다 (go in) and 나오다 (come out).

T1-548.m: to come out, to get out; to appear
T1-548.x: My friend came out of the room.
T1-548.e: 나다 (come out) + 오다 (come); opposite of 들어오다. 나가다 = go out.

T1-549.x: I go up to the third floor by the stairs.
T1-549.e: 오르다 (rise) + 가다 (go); 올라오다 = come up. Opposite: 내려가다.
T1-549.t: Also used for going up to Seoul from other regions: 서울에 올라가요.

T1-550.x: I take the elevator down to the first floor.
T1-550.e: 내리다 (come down, get off) + 가다 (go); 내려오다 = come down. Opposite: 올라가다.

T1-551.x: I'll go back to my hometown during the vacation.
T1-551.t: 돌아가시다 (honorific) also politely means 'to pass away'.

T1-552.ex: 아버지는 저녁 일곱 시에 집에 돌아와요.
T1-552.x: My father comes back home at seven in the evening.
T1-552.e: 돌다 (turn) + 오다 (come) — 'turn and come back'; pairs with 돌아가다.

T1-553.m: to attend (school, work) regularly; to go around
T1-553.x: My younger sibling goes to high school.
T1-553.t: Use 다니다 for regular attendance: 회사에 다녀요 = 'I work at a company,' not just one trip.

T1-554.x: I sent a birthday present to my friend.
T1-554.e: Two uses: 문자를 보내다 = send a text; 시간을 보내다 = spend time.
T1-554.t: 주말 잘 보내세요! = 'Have a nice weekend!'

T1-555.forms: 열어요 · 열었어요 · 열 거예요 · 여세요 (ㄹ drops)
T1-555.x: It's hot. Please open the window.
T1-555.t: ㄹ drops before ㅅ, ㄴ, ㅂ: 여세요, 여는 시간 (opening time).

T1-556.x: Be sure to close the door when you leave.
T1-556.e: Opposite of 열다 (open). Don't mix it up with 닦다 (wipe) — similar spelling.
T1-556.t: Regular verb — not ㄷ irregular like 듣다. 닫다 → 닫아요.

T1-557.m: to turn on, to switch on (lights, devices)
T1-557.x: The room is dark. Please turn on the light.
T1-557.e: Opposite: 끄다 (turn off). 불을 켜다 = turn on the light.

T1-558.forms: 꺼요 · 껐어요 · 끌 거예요 · 끄세요 (ㅡ drops)
T1-558.m: to turn off, to switch off; to put out (a fire)
T1-558.x: I turn off the TV before I go to sleep.
T1-558.e: Opposite of 켜다. 불을 끄다 = turn off the light, or put out a fire.
T1-558.t: ㅡ drops before 어: 끄 + 어요 → 꺼요.

T1-559.m: to look for, to search; to find; to withdraw (money)
T1-559.x: I'm looking for my bag right now.
T1-559.e: Also 'withdraw money': 돈을 찾다. 찾아보다 = look something up.
T1-559.t: 찾다 covers both 'look for' and 'find'; context decides. 찾았어요! = 'Found it!'

T1-560.x: I lost my wallet on the subway.
T1-560.e: 잃다 (lose) + 버리다 (throw away), adding a 'gone for good' feel.
T1-560.t: Pronounced [이러버리다]. Don't confuse with 잊어버리다 'to forget'.

T1-561.forms: 만들어요 · 만들었어요 · 만들 거예요 · 만드세요 (ㄹ drops)
T1-561.m: to make, to create; to cook
T1-561.x: I made gimbap with my mom on the weekend.
T1-561.e: Also used for cooking: 김밥을 만들다 = make gimbap.
T1-561.t: ㄹ drops before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ: 만드세요, 만듭니다, 만드는 법 (how to make).

T1-562.t: Pronounced [시자카다]. Works both ways: 수업이 시작해요 / 수업을 시작해요.

T1-563.m: to end, to be over, to finish
T1-563.x: The meeting ended at five o'clock.
T1-563.t: Pronounced [끈나다]. 끝나다 = something ends; 끝내다 = you finish something.

T1-564.m: to think; to consider; to remember
T1-564.x: I think that movie is interesting.
T1-564.e: 생각 (thought) + 하다 (do); 생각나다 = something comes to mind.

T1-565.m: to talk, to tell, to chat
T1-565.x: I talked with my friend for a long time at a café.
T1-565.e: 이야기 (story, talk) + 하다 (do); often shortened to 얘기하다 in speech.

T1-566.forms: 물어요 · 물었어요 · 물을 거예요 · 물으세요 (ㄷ irregular)
T1-566.x: I didn't know the way, so I asked a police officer.
T1-566.t: ㄷ → ㄹ before a vowel: 물어요. Everyday speech prefers 물어보다.

T1-567.x: I answered the teacher's question in a loud voice.

T1-568.x: The baby looks at its mom and smiles.
T1-568.e: Covers both laughing and smiling; 웃음 = laughter, 웃기다 = to be funny.

T1-569.forms: 울어요 · 울었어요 · 울 거예요 · 우세요 (ㄹ drops)
T1-569.m: to cry, to weep; to sing (birds), to make a sound (animals)
T1-569.x: I cried a lot after watching a sad movie.
T1-569.e: Also for animal and bird sounds; 울음 = crying. Don't confuse with 웃다 (laugh).
T1-569.t: ㄹ drops before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ: 우세요, 우는 아이 (a crying child).

T1-570.x: I sang together with my friends at a karaoke room.
T1-570.e: 노래 (song) + 하다 (do); 노래방 = karaoke, literally 'song room'.
T1-570.t: Also common: 노래를 부르다 'to sing a song'; 노래를 잘하다 'to sing well'.

T1-571.x: I danced with my friends at the party.
T1-571.e: 춤 (dance) + 추다 (to dance) — 춤 comes from 추다 itself.

T1-572.m: to travel, to take a trip
T1-572.x: I traveled around Jeju Island last summer.
T1-572.t: Place + 을/를 여행하다 (travel around), or place + 에 여행을 가다 (go on a trip to).

T1-573.m: to take a walk, to stroll
T1-573.x: After dinner, I take a walk in the park.
T1-573.e: Sino-Korean, but 책 here isn't 'book' — just learn 산책 (a walk) whole.

T1-574.x: I went shopping at the department store on the weekend.
T1-574.e: From English 'shopping' + 하다 (do); 쇼핑몰 = shopping mall.

T1-575.e: 준비 (preparation) + 하다 (do); 준비됐어요? = Are you ready?

T1-576.forms: 도와요 · 도왔어요 · 도울 거예요 · 도우세요 (ㅂ irregular)
T1-576.x: I help my mother with her work every weekend.
T1-576.t: ㅂ irregular: ㅂ becomes 오/우 — 돕다 is one of the few that become 와: 도와요.

T1-577.e: 돕다 (help) + 주다 (give) — helping as a favor.
T1-577.t: 도와주세요! is the natural way to say 'Help me, please!'

T1-578.x: I borrowed an umbrella from a friend.
T1-578.t: 빌리다 = borrow; 빌려주다 = lend. 펜 좀 빌려주세요 'Could you lend me a pen?'

T1-579.m: to change, to exchange, to switch
T1-579.ex: 이 옷을 큰 사이즈로 바꿔 주세요.
T1-579.x: Please exchange these clothes for a bigger size.
T1-579.e: Also exchange: 돈을 바꾸다 = exchange money; 바꿔 주세요 = please switch it.

T1-580.forms: 골라요 · 골랐어요 · 고를 거예요 · 고르세요 (르 irregular)
T1-580.m: to choose, to pick, to select
T1-580.t: 르 irregular: 르 + 아 → ㄹ라 — 고르다 → 골라요.

T1-581.x: I ordered two coffees and a cake.
T1-581.e: Literally 'noting in writing' — picture a waiter writing down your order.
T1-581.t: Waiters ask: 주문하시겠어요? 'Are you ready to order?'

T1-582.t: At a restaurant, 계산해 주세요 = 'The check, please.' Pronounced [게산하다].

T1-583.m: to take (time); to catch (a cold); to hang (be hung)
T1-583.x: It takes thirty minutes from home to school.
T1-583.e: Passive of 걸다 (hang); 감기에 걸리다 = catch a cold.
T1-583.t: Ask duration: 얼마나 걸려요? 'How long does it take?'

T1-584.forms: 들어요 · 들었어요 · 들 거예요 · 드세요 (ㄹ drops)
T1-584.m: to hold, to carry (in the hand); to lift
T1-584.ex: 이 가방이 무거워요. 같이 들어 주세요.
T1-584.x: This bag is heavy. Please carry it with me.
T1-584.e: Watch out: other 들다 mean 'enter' (as in 들어가다) and 'cost' (돈이 들다).
T1-584.t: Careful: 들어요 can also come from 듣다 'listen', and 드세요 can mean 'please eat' (드시다).

T1-585.m: to put, to place, to set down
T1-585.x: Please put your bag on the chair.
T1-585.e: Put down; 놓고 오다 = to leave something behind.

T1-586.m: to put in, to insert, to add
T1-586.x: Do you put sugar in your coffee?
T1-586.e: Opposite: 빼다 (take out). 설탕을 넣다 = add sugar.

T1-587.m: to have, to own; to take, to hold
T1-587.ex: 저는 한국 돈을 조금 가지고 있어요.
T1-587.x: I have a little Korean money.
T1-587.t: Common pattern: 가지고 있다 'to have (on you)'. Often shortened to 갖다.

T1-588.m: to take (something) along, to take away
T1-588.x: It's raining. Take an umbrella with you.
T1-588.e: 가지다 (hold) + 가다 (go) — carry it away; compare 가져오다 (bring).
T1-588.t: Takes things away from where you are; for people use 데려가다.
