T1-589.x: Be sure to bring your textbook tomorrow.
T1-589.e: 가지다 (hold) + 오다 (come) — carry it here; compare 가져가다 (take).

T1-590.m: to wipe, to clean, to polish; to brush (teeth)
T1-590.x: I brush my teeth after eating.
T1-590.e: 이를 닦다 = brush your teeth. Don't confuse with 닫다 (close).

T1-591.forms: 잘라요 · 잘랐어요 · 자를 거예요 · 자르세요 (르 irregular)
T1-591.x: I got my hair cut at the hair salon yesterday.
T1-591.t: 르 irregular: 자르 + 아요 → 잘라요. 머리를 잘랐어요 also means 'I got a haircut.'

T1-592.x: The child drew a cat on paper.
T1-592.e: Related to 그림 (picture, drawing). A different 그리다 means 'to miss, long for'.

T1-593.m: to play (tennis, piano, etc.); to hit, to strike
T1-593.x: I play tennis with my friend on weekends.
T1-593.e: Hitting actions: 테니스를 치다 (play tennis), 피아노를 치다 (play piano), 박수를 치다 (clap).
T1-593.t: Use 치다 for games hit with hands/rackets and for piano/guitar; 축구 uses 하다.

T1-594.m: to take (a photo); to stamp; to dip
T1-594.x: Let's take a photo together here.
T1-594.e: Press-down actions: 사진을 찍다 (take a photo), 소스에 찍다 (dip in sauce).

T1-595.x: My older sister got married last year.
T1-595.t: 'Marry someone' → 사람하고/와 결혼하다 (not 을/를). 'Are you married?' → 결혼했어요?

T1-596.x: I was born in Seoul in 1998.
T1-596.e: Ends in 나다 (come out, appear); 태어난 날 = birthday.

T1-597.x: The flowers died because I didn't water them.
T1-597.e: 죽 also means rice porridge — a different word.
T1-597.t: For elders and respected people use 돌아가시다. Casual slang: 배고파 죽겠어요 'I'm starving.'

T1-598.m: to get hurt, to be injured
T1-598.x: I hurt my leg while playing soccer.
T1-598.e: Sounds exactly like 닫히다 (to be closed) — context tells them apart.

T1-599.forms: 누워요 · 누웠어요 · 누울 거예요 · 누우세요 (ㅂ irregular)
T1-599.x: I was tired, so I lay down on the bed.
T1-599.e: Irregular: 누워요; 누워 있다 = to be lying down.

T1-601.x: I forgot my friend's phone number.
T1-601.t: Pronounced [이저버리다]. Don't mix up with 잃어버리다 'to lose (an object)'.

T1-602.x: I practice Korean pronunciation every day.

T1-603.x: I understood the teacher's explanation well.
T1-603.e: Literally 'solve the reason' — figure out how something works.
T1-603.t: Didn't catch something? 잘 모르겠어요 is more natural than 이해 못 해요 in daily talk.

T1-604.m: to depart, to leave, to set off
T1-604.x: The train departs from Seoul Station at ten.
T1-604.e: Literally 'go out and set off'; opposite: 도착하다 (arrive).

T1-605.x: I just arrived at the airport.
T1-605.e: Literally 'reach and arrive'; opposite of 출발하다 (depart).
T1-605.t: Pronounced [도차카다]. Destination takes 에: 집에 도착했어요.

T1-606.x: My father drives to work every day.
T1-606.t: Drive a car: 차를 운전하다. Common goodbye: 운전 조심하세요 'Drive safely.'

T1-607.x: I'm moving to a new apartment next month.
T1-607.e: Both parts mean 'move' — moving house. 이사 가다 = to move away.

T1-608.x: I invited my friends to my birthday party.

T1-609.m: to promise; to make plans (to meet)
T1-609.x: I made plans to meet my friend tomorrow.
T1-609.t: Pronounced [약쏘카다]. 약속 is also a social appointment: 오늘 약속이 있어요 'I have plans today.'

T1-610.m: to be seen, to be visible; to show
T1-610.x: You can see Namsan Tower through the window.
T1-610.t: The thing seen takes 이/가: 산이 보여요. 'Show me' → 보여 주세요.

T1-611.m: to be heard, to be audible
T1-611.x: I can hear music from outside.
T1-611.e: Passive of 듣다 (hear); 잘 들려요? = Can you hear me?
T1-611.t: The sound takes 이/가: 소리가 들려요. On the phone: 잘 안 들려요 'I can't hear you well.'

T1-612.forms: 축하해요 · 축하했어요 · 축하할 거예요 · 축하해 주세요

T1-613.x: Cross the street when the light is green.
T1-613.e: 길을 건너다 = cross the street; 건너편 = the other side.

T1-614.x: I booked the restaurant for seven in the evening.

T1-615.m: to look around, to sightsee, to watch (for fun)
T1-615.x: I looked around Myeongdong on the weekend.
T1-615.e: Watching for fun — sightseeing, window shopping; 구경꾼 = onlooker.
T1-615.t: In shops, 그냥 구경하고 있어요 = 'I'm just looking.'

T1-616.forms: 싸워요 · 싸웠어요 · 싸울 거예요 · 싸우지 마세요
T1-616.m: to fight, to argue, to quarrel
T1-616.x: I had a fight with my younger sibling yesterday.
T1-616.e: 싸움 = a fight; 싸우지 마! = Don't fight!

T1-618.ex: 어제 축구 경기에서 우리 팀이 졌어요.
T1-618.x: Our team lost the soccer match yesterday.
T1-618.e: Opposite of 이기다. A different 지다 means 'set': 해가 지다 = the sun sets.

T1-619.e: Honorific for both eating and drinking.
T1-619.t: Use for others you respect, never yourself. 맛있게 드세요 = 'Enjoy your meal.'

T1-620.x: Grandpa is sleeping in his room now.
T1-620.t: 안녕히 주무세요 = 'Good night' to elders. Never use 주무시다 about yourself.

T1-621.m: to be, to stay, to exist (honorific of 있다 for people)
T1-621.x: My mother is at home now.
T1-621.e: Honorific of 있다 for people; 안녕히 계세요 = Goodbye (to someone staying).
T1-621.t: 계시다 is for a respected person's location; 'have' uses 있으시다: 시간 있으세요?

T1-622.x: The teacher said there's a test tomorrow.
T1-622.e: 말씀 (polite word for 말, speech) + 하시다.

T1-623.x: I graduate from university next February.
T1-623.t: Pronounced [조러파다]. School takes 을/를: 고등학교를 졸업했어요.

T1-624.m: to enter (a school), to be admitted
T1-624.x: My younger sibling started elementary school this year.
T1-624.t: Pronounced [이파카다]. School takes 에: 대학교에 입학하다.

T1-625.m: to get along, to be doing (well/badly); to spend (time), to live
T1-625.x: How are you doing these days?
T1-625.e: 잘 지내요? = 'How are you doing?' — a very common greeting.
T1-625.t: 잘 지냈어요? = 'How have you been?' — a very common greeting when you meet someone after a while.

T1-626.e: 좋아요 = 'good!' or 'I like it'; 좋아하다 = to like.
T1-626.t: Pronounced [조타]; the ㅎ is silent before a vowel: 좋아요 [조아요].

T1-627.x: Smoking is bad for your health.
T1-627.e: 나빠요 (the ㅡ drops). 나쁜 남자 'bad boy' is a classic K-drama type.

T1-628.t: For people, 키가 커요 means 'is tall' (literally 'height is big').

T1-629.x: My room is a bit small.
T1-629.t: 작다 = small in size; 적다 = few or little in amount. Don't mix them up!

T1-630.x: There are really a lot of people in Myeongdong.
T1-630.e: 많이 = a lot; hosts say 많이 드세요 'eat a lot!'
T1-630.t: Pronounced [만타]; the ㅎ is silent before a vowel: 많아요 [마나요].

T1-631.x: This restaurant has few customers today.
T1-631.t: A different verb 적다 means 'to write down'.

T1-632.x: My younger sibling has long hair.
T1-632.e: 길이 = length. 길 (road) is a separate word.

T1-633.x: These pants are too short for me.
T1-633.e: Opposite of 길다; 짧은 머리 = short hair.
T1-633.t: Pronounced [짤따]; 짧아요 [짤바요]. For a short person, say 키가 작다, not 짧다.

T1-635.x: This chair is a little low.
T1-635.t: Don't confuse with the noun 낮 'daytime'. Pronounced [낟따].

T1-636.x: Our school's playground is very spacious.

T1-637.e: Opposite of 넓다. 방이 좁아요 = the room is cramped.

T1-638.t: ㅂ irregular: ㅂ becomes 우 before a vowel — 무겁다 → 무거워요.

T1-639.e: ㅂ becomes 우: 가벼워요. Opposite: 무겁다.

T1-640.x: The subway is faster than the bus.
T1-640.e: 빨리 = quickly — think of Korea's famous 빨리빨리 ('hurry hurry') culture.
T1-640.t: 르 irregular: 르 + 아요 becomes 라요 with an extra ㄹ — 빠르다 → 빨라요.

T1-641.x: The internet at our house is too slow.
T1-641.e: Opposite of 빠르다. For 'slowly' Koreans usually say 천천히.

T1-642.x: It's a bit far from home to the office.
T1-642.e: ㄹ drops before ㄴ: 먼 곳 (a far place). Opposite: 가깝다.
T1-642.t: Common pattern: A에서 B까지 멀어요 = It's far from A to B.

T1-643.x: The school is very close to my house.

T1-644.e: 비싸요! = 'It's expensive!' — handy at markets. Opposite: 싸다.

T1-645.x: Fruit is cheap at the market.
T1-645.e: 쌈 (lettuce wraps) comes from the other 싸다.
T1-645.t: A different verb 싸다 means 'to pack, to wrap' (e.g. 짐을 싸다).

T1-646.x: This kimchi stew is really delicious.
T1-646.e: 맛 (taste) + 있다 (have) = 'has taste'. Sounds like 마싣따.
T1-646.t: Words ending in 있다/없다 take -는 before a noun: 맛있는 음식 (not 맛있은).

T1-647.x: This bread doesn't taste very good.

T1-648.t: In casual speech it's often shortened to 재밌다 / 재밌어요.

T1-649.x: That movie was kind of boring.

T1-650.e: ㅂ becomes 우: 쉬워요. Opposite: 어렵다.

T1-651.x: Korean grammar is a bit difficult.
T1-651.t: ㅂ irregular: 어렵다 → 어려워요, 어려운 문제 (a difficult question).

T1-652.x: Summer in Korea is really hot.
T1-652.t: 덥다 is for weather or feeling hot; for hot food or objects use 뜨겁다.

T1-653.x: It's cold today because the wind is blowing.
T1-653.t: 춥다 is for weather or feeling cold; for cold drinks or objects use 차갑다.

T1-654.x: The weather is warm in spring.
T1-654.t: Also used for people: 따뜻한 사람 = a warm-hearted person. Pronounced [따뜨타다].

T1-655.ex: 더운 날에는 시원한 물을 마시고 싶어요.
T1-655.x: On hot days I want to drink cool water.
T1-655.e: Koreans also say 시원하다 after a good massage.
T1-655.t: Koreans also say 시원해요 about hot soup — meaning 'refreshing, satisfying'.

T1-656.e: For things hot to the touch (coffee, soup). Hot weather is 덥다.

T1-657.e: For things cold to the touch; cold weather is 춥다. 차가운 사람 = a cold person.

T1-658.t: Pronounced [막따], but 맑아요 [말가요] — the ㄹ comes back before a vowel.

T1-659.x: The weather is a bit cloudy today.
T1-659.e: 흐림 = 'cloudy' on weather forecasts. Opposite: 맑다.

T1-660.x: The flowers in the park are really pretty.
T1-660.e: 예뻐요! = 'You're pretty / It's pretty!' — a very common compliment.
T1-660.t: ㅡ drops before 아/어: 예쁘다 → 예뻐요.

T1-661.t: 아름답다 sounds more elegant than 예쁘다 — often used for scenery, music or a person's heart.

T1-662.e: 멋 (style, charm) + 있다 (have). 멋져요! means the same.

T1-663.x: My friend's puppy is really cute.
T1-663.e: 귀여워요! Acting cute is called 애교 (aegyo), big in K-pop.

T1-664.t: 착하다 describes someone's good character; 친절하다 describes kind behavior toward others. Pronounced [차카다].

T1-665.x: The staff at that store are really friendly.

T1-666.x: I'm busy these days because I have a lot of work.

T1-667.x: I'm so tired because I went to bed late yesterday.
T1-667.e: 피곤 (fatigue) + 하다: 'tired and weary'. 피곤해요 = I'm tired.

T1-668.x: My legs hurt from climbing so many stairs.
T1-668.t: Body part + 이/가 아파요 = my ___ hurts: 배가 아파요 'My stomach hurts.'

T1-669.x: I'm hungry because I didn't eat breakfast.
T1-669.e: 배 (stomach) + 고프다 (empty). 배 also means pear and boat.
T1-669.t: Often said with a particle: 배가 고파요.

T1-670.x: I ate too much, so I'm full.
T1-670.t: 르 irregular: 배부르다 → 배불러요. Also said 배가 불러요.

T1-671.x: I'm really happy to see my friend again.
T1-671.e: 기뻐요 = I'm glad. 기쁨 = joy. Opposite: 슬프다.

T1-673.x: I'm happy when I'm with my family.
T1-673.t: Pronounced [행보카다]. 행복하세요! = 'Be happy!' — a common warm wish.

T1-674.x: Traveling with my friends was really fun.
T1-674.e: 즐거운 시간 보내세요 = 'Have a good time!'
T1-674.t: 즐거운 주말 보내세요! = 'Have a nice weekend!'

T1-675.e: Means both 'scary' and 'scared'. 무서운 영화 = horror movie.
T1-675.t: The thing you fear takes 이/가: 저는 개가 무서워요 'I'm scared of dogs.'

T1-676.x: The hotel room is very clean.

T1-678.e: 조용히 하세요 is a common library sign.

T1-679.e: 시끄러워! = 'It's so loud! / Be quiet!' — often heard in dramas.

T1-681.x: This chair is a little uncomfortable.

T1-682.x: The tteokbokki is a bit spicy.
T1-682.e: 매워요! When ordering, ask for 덜 맵게 (less spicy).
T1-682.t: Useful at restaurants: 안 맵게 해 주세요 = 'Please make it not spicy.'

T1-683.e: 달콤하다 = sweet (cuter-sounding). 달 (moon) is a separate word.
T1-683.t: ㄹ drops before ㄴ: 단 음식 = sweet food.

T1-684.x: The soup is a little salty.
T1-684.e: 짜요 = it's salty. A different 짜다 means 'to squeeze'.

T1-685.t: Same spelling as the verb 쓰다 'to write, to use, to wear (a hat)' — context tells you which.

T1-686.t: Pronounced [점따]; 젊어요 [절머요]. 젊다 is for adults; use 어리다 for children.

T1-687.x: My younger sibling is still young.
T1-687.e: For kids: 어린이 = child, and 어린이날 = Children's Day (May 5).
T1-687.t: Don't confuse 어려요 (is young) with 어려워요 (is difficult, from 어렵다).

T1-688.x: My friend and I are the same age.
T1-688.t: Pronounced [갇따]; 같아요 [가타요]. The adverb 같이 'together' is pronounced [가치].

T1-689.x: Korean and English are very different.
T1-689.e: 달라요. Koreans often say 틀리다 (wrong) when they mean 다르다.
T1-689.t: The modifier 다른 also means 'other': 다른 사람 = another person.

T1-690.m: okay, all right, fine; not bad, decent
T1-690.x: The color of these clothes looks nice.
T1-690.e: Shortened from 괜하지 않다. 괜찮아요 = 'It's okay.'
T1-690.t: 괜찮아요 can also politely decline an offer: 'No thanks, I'm fine.' Pronounced [괜찬타].

T1-691.x: This restaurant is famous for its bibimbap.
T1-691.e: Literally 'having a name' — famous. 유명한 가수 = a famous singer.
T1-691.t: N(으)로 유명하다 = to be famous for N.

T1-692.x: Health is the most important thing.

T1-693.t: The needed thing takes 이/가, not 을/를: 돈이 필요해요. Pronounced [피료하다].

T1-695.x: This room is bright because the window is big.
T1-695.t: Pronounced [박따], but 밝아요 [발가요]. 밝은 성격 = a cheerful personality.

T1-696.x: This road is dark at night.

T1-697.x: Maple leaves turn red in autumn.
T1-697.t: ㅎ irregular: ㅎ drops and 아 becomes 애 — 빨갛다 → 빨개요, 빨간 사과.

T1-698.x: The sky is really blue today.
T1-698.t: A green traffic light is called 파란불 in Korean.

T1-699.x: Ginkgo leaves are yellow in autumn.
T1-699.e: 노란색 = the color yellow. The ㅎ drops: 노란 옷.

T1-700.x: It snowed, so the streets are white.
T1-700.e: 하얀 눈 = white snow. 흰색 also means white.
T1-700.t: Note the spelling: 하얗다 → 하얘요 (with ㅒ), not 하애요.

T1-701.e: 까만색 = black. 검은색 is another common word for black.

T1-702.e: 싫어요! = 'No, I don't want to.' 싫어하다 = to dislike.
T1-702.t: 싫다 takes 이/가 (비가 싫어요); 싫어하다 takes 을/를 (비를 싫어해요). Pronounced [실타]; 싫어요 [시러요].

T1-703.m: glad (to see/meet), pleased, nice to meet
T1-703.t: Formal greeting: 만나서 반갑습니다. Use it for meeting someone, not for being happy in general (that's 기쁘다).

T1-704.x: Thank you so much for helping me.
T1-704.e: 고맙습니다 is the native 'thank you'; 감사합니다 is its Sino-Korean twin.

T1-705.t: To elders or strangers, 죄송합니다 is more polite than 미안해요.

T1-706.x: I'm bored because I'm alone on the weekend.
T1-706.e: Also means 'a bit bland' for food. 심심해요 = I'm bored.
T1-706.t: 심심하다 = bored because there's nothing to do; a boring movie is 재미없다.

T1-707.t: Also works as a verb 'to be late for': 학교에 늦었어요 = I was late for school.

T1-708.forms: 아주 + adjective/verb: 아주 좋아요, 아주 잘해요
T1-708.x: The food at this restaurant is very delicious.
T1-708.e: 아주 좋아요 = very good. A bit more neutral than 너무 or 진짜.

T1-709.forms: 정말 + adjective/verb: 정말 좋아요; as a question: 정말요?
T1-709.e: 정 right + native 말 (words) — literally 'right words'.
T1-709.t: 정말요? means 'Really?' — a handy reaction in conversation.

T1-710.forms: 진짜 + adjective/verb: 진짜 맛있어요; as a question: 진짜요?
T1-710.t: More casual than 정말; very common in everyday speech.

T1-711.forms: 너무 + adjective/verb: 너무 비싸요, 너무 좋아요
T1-711.e: From 넘다 (to go over) — 'too much'; now often just means 'so, really'.
T1-711.t: Originally negative ('too much'), but now also used positively: 너무 좋아요 = I love it.

T1-712.forms: short form: 좀 · 조금 + verb/adjective: 조금 어려워요
T1-712.m: a little, a bit; a little while
T1-712.x: I can speak a little Korean.
T1-712.e: Shortened to 좀 in everyday speech.

T1-713.forms: short for 조금 · softener in requests: 좀 주세요, 좀 도와주세요
T1-713.m: a little, a bit; please (softens a request)
T1-713.x: Could I have some water, please?
T1-713.e: Short for 조금. Also softens requests: 물 좀 주세요 (Some water, please).
T1-713.t: Adding 좀 makes requests sound softer and more polite.

T1-714.forms: 많이 + verb: 많이 먹어요 · 많이 드세요 (eat a lot — said to guests)
T1-714.e: From 많다 (to be many). 많이 드세요 = 'Eat a lot!' — a host's warm urging.

T1-715.forms: 다 + verb: 다 먹었어요, 다 왔어요

T1-716.forms: 모두 + verb: 모두 왔어요 · also a noun: 모두가
T1-716.x: All the students came to the classroom.
T1-716.e: Also a noun: 모두 = everyone. 여러분 모두 = all of you.

T1-717.x: Shall we watch a movie together this weekend?

T1-718.x: I live together with my parents.
T1-718.t: Same meaning as 같이, but a bit more formal or written.

T1-719.forms: 혼자 + verb: 혼자 살아요 · also a noun: 혼자서
T1-719.e: 혼자서 = by oneself; slang 혼밥 (혼자 + 밥) = eating alone.

T1-720.forms: 자주 + verb: 자주 가요, 자주 만나요
T1-720.x: I often go to that café.

T1-721.x: I sometimes go hiking on weekends.

T1-722.e: Both parts mean 'constant' — doubled up for 'always'.

T1-723.forms: 보통 + verb: 보통 일곱 시에 일어나요 · also a noun: 보통이에요 (it's average)
T1-723.x: I usually go to work by subway.

T1-724.e: 벌써 = already; 아직 = still, not yet.
T1-724.t: 벌써 often shows surprise that something happened sooner than expected.

T1-725.forms: 아직 + negative: 아직 안 왔어요 · 아직 + positive: 아직 자요 (still)
T1-725.e: 아직 안 했어요 = I haven't done it yet.
T1-725.t: With a negative it means 'not yet'; with a positive it means 'still'.

T1-726.forms: 곧 + verb: 곧 도착해요, 곧 시작할 거예요

T1-727.forms: 다시 + verb: 다시 말해 주세요, 다시 만나요
T1-727.x: Please say it one more time.
T1-727.e: 다시 한번 = one more time; 다시 만나요 = see you again.
T1-727.t: 다시 = again (redo/repeat); 또 = again (another occurrence, often unwanted).

T1-728.forms: 또 + verb: 또 왔어요 · 또 만나요 (see you again)
T1-728.e: 또 봐요 = See you again. 또 + 는 = 또는 (or).

T1-729.forms: 먼저 + verb: 먼저 가세요, 먼저 드세요
T1-729.t: 먼저 드세요 = 'Please eat first / go ahead.' A polite phrase you'll hear often.

T1-730.forms: 나중에 + verb: 나중에 전화할게요 · 나중에 봐요 (see you later)
T1-730.x: I'm busy now. I'll call you later.
T1-730.e: 나중 (later time) + 에 (at). 나중에 봐요 = See you later.

T1-731.forms: 빨리 + verb: 빨리 와요 · 빨리빨리 (hurry, hurry)
T1-731.t: 빨리빨리 ('quick quick') is a famous phrase describing Korea's fast-paced culture.

T1-732.forms: 천천히 + verb: 천천히 말해 주세요, 천천히 드세요
T1-732.x: Please speak a little more slowly.
T1-732.t: 천천히 드세요 = 'Take your time eating' — a kind thing to say to guests.

T1-733.forms: 잘 + verb: 잘 먹겠습니다 · 잘 자요 · 잘하다 (to be good at)
T1-733.t: Many set phrases: 잘 먹겠습니다 (before eating), 잘 지내요? (how are you?).

T1-734.forms: 못 + verb: 못 가요 · long form: 가지 못해요
T1-734.e: As a noun, 못 also means nail.
T1-734.t: 못 = can't (inability); 안 = don't (choice). 못 가요 'I can't go' vs 안 가요 'I'm not going'.

T1-735.forms: 안 + verb/adjective: 안 가요, 안 비싸요 · long form: 가지 않아요
T1-735.e: Short for 아니. 안 = don't (choice); 못 = can't (inability).
T1-735.t: With 하다 verbs, 안 goes before 하다: 공부 안 해요, not 안 공부해요.

T1-736.forms: 일찍 + verb: 일찍 일어나요, 일찍 자요
T1-736.x: I have to get up early tomorrow.
T1-736.e: Opposite of 늦게 (late). 일찍 일어나요 = I get up early.
T1-736.t: 일찍 = early (time); 빨리 = quickly (speed). Don't mix them up.

T1-737.forms: 늦게 + verb: 늦게 자요, 늦게 와요
T1-737.x: I went to bed late last night.
T1-737.e: 늦다 (to be late) + -게 (adverb ending). Opposite: 일찍 (early).

T1-738.forms: 제일 + adjective: 제일 좋아요 · (noun) 중에서 제일 …
T1-738.x: I like kimchi stew the most.
T1-738.t: Pattern: A 중에서 B가 제일 … = 'Among A, B is the most …'.

T1-739.forms: 더 + adjective/verb: 더 커요 · A보다 B가 더 …
T1-739.x: My younger sibling is taller than me.

T1-740.forms: 꼭 + verb: 꼭 오세요, 꼭 가고 싶어요
T1-740.x: Please be sure to come again next time.
T1-740.e: 꼭 오세요 = Be sure to come; 꼭 안아요 = hug tight.

T1-741.forms: 아마 + -(으)ㄹ 거예요: 아마 비가 올 거예요
T1-741.e: 아마 비가 올 거예요 (It'll probably rain).
T1-741.t: Usually paired with a guess ending like -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

T1-742.forms: 그냥 + verb: 그냥 가요 · as an answer: 그냥요 (just because)
T1-742.m: just, simply; as it is, without any reason
T1-742.x: Today I just want to rest at home.
T1-742.t: 왜요? — 그냥요. ('Why?' — 'Just because.') Very common in speech.

T1-743.forms: 오래 + verb: 오래 기다렸어요 · 오래간만이에요 (long time no see)
T1-743.e: Related to 오랜만이에요 = Long time no see.

T1-744.forms: 별로 + negative: 별로 안 좋아해요 · alone: 별로예요 (not great)
T1-744.ex: 저는 매운 음식을 별로 안 좋아해요.
T1-744.x: I don't really like spicy food.
T1-744.e: 별 special + 로 — 'not specially'. Not 별 (star).
T1-744.t: Almost always used with a negative. 별로예요 on its own means 'It's not that good.'

T1-745.forms: 바로 + verb: 바로 가요 · 바로 옆 (right next to)
T1-745.m: right away, immediately; right, exactly, directly
T1-745.x: I went home right after class ended.
T1-745.e: 바로 = right away; 바로 여기 = right here.
T1-745.t: Also for location: 은행 바로 옆에 있어요 = It's right next to the bank.

T1-746.forms: 열심히 + verb: 열심히 공부해요, 열심히 일해요
T1-746.x: I'm studying hard because of the exam.
T1-746.e: Literally 'with a hot heart' — 열심 + 히 (-ly). 열심히 공부해요 = study hard.

T1-747.forms: 계속 + verb: 계속 비가 와요 · verb: 계속하다 (to continue)
T1-747.x: It's been raining nonstop since morning.
T1-747.e: Both parts mean 'continue'. 계속 가세요 = Keep going.

T1-748.forms: 잠깐 + verb: 잠깐 기다리세요 · 잠깐만요! (just a moment!)
T1-748.m: for a moment, briefly; a moment (noun)
T1-748.t: 잠깐만요! also works as 'Excuse me' to get past people in a crowd.

T1-749.forms: 얼마나 + adjective: 얼마나 걸려요?, 얼마나 커요?
T1-749.x: How long does it take from home to school?
T1-749.t: 얼마예요? asks a price; 얼마나 asks degree: 얼마나 걸려요? = How long does it take?

T1-750.forms: starts a sentence: A. 그리고 B. · within a sentence use -고
T1-750.ex: 저는 빵을 샀어요. 그리고 우유도 샀어요.
T1-750.x: I bought bread. And I also bought milk.
T1-750.e: From 그리하다 (to do so) + -고 (and). 그 'that' also starts 그래서, 그런데.
T1-750.t: 그리고 links sentences; to join nouns use 하고 or 와/과.

T1-751.forms: casual short form: 근데 · starts a sentence
T1-751.ex: 이 옷이 예뻐요. 그런데 좀 비싸요.
T1-751.x: These clothes are pretty. But they're a bit expensive.
T1-751.t: Also used to change the topic: 'By the way…'. In speech it's often shortened to 근데.

T1-752.forms: starts a sentence: A. 그래서 B. · within a sentence use -아/어서
T1-752.ex: 어제 너무 피곤했어요. 그래서 일찍 잤어요.
T1-752.x: I was very tired yesterday. So I went to bed early.
T1-752.e: From 그러하다 (to be so) + -어서 (so). 그래서요? = And then? / So?

T1-753.forms: written/formal; in speech use 하지만 or 그런데
T1-753.ex: 그 식당은 비쌉니다. 그러나 음식이 맛있습니다.
T1-753.x: That restaurant is expensive. However, the food is delicious.
T1-753.e: From 그러하다 (to be so) + -나 (but). More written than 하지만 or 그런데.
T1-753.t: Mostly used in writing and formal speeches.

T1-754.forms: starts a sentence: A. 하지만 B. · within a sentence use -지만
T1-754.x: Korean is difficult. But it's fun.

T1-755.forms: short for 그러면 · reply: 그럼요! (of course!)
T1-755.m: then, in that case; of course
T1-755.x: It's raining? Then I'll stay home.
T1-755.e: Short for 그러면 (if so). 그럼요! = Of course!
T1-755.t: 그럼 안녕히 계세요 = 'Well then, goodbye.' A natural way to end a conversation.

T1-756.forms: between nouns: A 또는 B · in speech often 아니면 or -(이)나
T1-756.x: Shall I get you coffee or tea?
T1-756.e: 또 (also) + 는. In casual speech 아니면 often replaces it.
T1-756.t: Somewhat formal; in conversation 커피나 차 is more common.

T1-757.forms: 은 after a consonant (책은) · 는 after a vowel (저는)
T1-757.e: 은 after a consonant (책은), 는 after a vowel (저는 = as for me).
T1-757.t: 은/는 marks what you're talking about; 이/가 marks new information. 'Who came?' → 누가 왔어요?

T1-758.forms: 이 after a consonant (책이) · 가 after a vowel (친구가) · 나/저/누구 + 가 → 내가/제가/누가
T1-758.x: There are many students in the classroom.
T1-758.e: 이 after a consonant (책이), 가 after a vowel (친구가).
T1-758.t: Watch the special forms: 나 + 가 = 내가, 저 + 가 = 제가, 누구 + 가 = 누가.

T1-759.forms: 을 after a consonant (밥을) · 를 after a vowel (커피를)
T1-759.x: I drink coffee in the morning.
T1-759.e: 을 after a consonant (밥을), 를 after a vowel (커피를).
T1-759.t: In casual speech it's often dropped or shortened: 뭘 (뭐를), 날 (나를).

T1-760.forms: place + 에 가다/오다/있다 (학교에 가요) · time + 에 (세 시에)
T1-760.x: I go to the library on Saturday.
T1-760.e: 학교에 가요 = I go to school; 세 시에 = at three o'clock.
T1-760.t: Use 에 with destinations and with 있다/없다; use 에서 for where an action happens. No 에 after 오늘, 내일, 어제.

T1-761.forms: place + 에서 + action verb (식당에서 먹어요) · starting point (집에서 학교까지)
T1-761.m: at, in (where an action happens); from
T1-761.x: I meet my friend at a café.
T1-761.e: 집에서 먹어요 = I eat at home.
T1-761.t: 어디에서 왔어요? = 'Where are you from?' Here 에서 means 'from'.

T1-762.x: I wrote a letter to my mother.
T1-762.e: Polite/written; 한테 is the casual version. 친구에게 = to a friend.
T1-762.t: For places or things use 에; for people and animals use 에게/한테.

T1-763.m: to (a person or animal); from (a person)
T1-763.x: I gave a present to my younger sibling.
T1-763.t: 한테 is the conversational version of 에게.

T1-764.forms: 과 after a consonant (빵과 우유) · 와 after a vowel (우유와 빵)
T1-764.e: 와 after a vowel (커피와), 과 after a consonant (빵과).
T1-764.t: 와/과 is more formal or written; in conversation 하고 or (이)랑 are more common.

T1-765.forms: same after consonant or vowel: 빵하고 우유 · (누구)하고 같이 (with someone)
T1-765.x: I watched a movie with my friend.
T1-765.e: From 하다 + -고. The everyday spoken 'and/with': 친구하고 영화 봐요.
T1-765.t: Easy to use: one form for every noun, no batchim rule.

T1-766.forms: same after consonant or vowel: 저도, 책도 · replaces 은/는, 이/가, 을/를
T1-766.t: 도 replaces subject/object particles: say 저도, not 저는도. But it follows 에/에서: 학교에도.

T1-767.forms: same after consonant or vowel: 물만, 하나만 · 만 can replace 이/가, 을/를
T1-767.e: 물만 주세요 = Just water, please. Different from 만 (ten thousand).

T1-768.forms: noun + 의 + noun (친구의 책) · 나의 → 내, 저의 → 제, 너의 → 네
T1-768.e: 나의 shortens to 내 (my), 저의 to 제.
T1-768.t: As a particle it's usually pronounced [에]. It's often dropped in speech: 친구 책.

T1-769.forms: 으로 after a consonant (손으로) · 로 after a vowel or ㄹ (버스로, 지하철로)
T1-769.x: I go to school by bus.
T1-769.e: 으로 after consonants (손으로), 로 after vowels (버스로).
T1-769.t: Words ending in ㄹ take 로, not 으로: 지하철로, 연필로.

T1-770.forms: time + 부터 (아홉 시부터) · often 부터 … 까지
T1-770.e: Probably from 붙다 (to stick). Pairs with 까지: 9시부터 5시까지 = from 9 to 5.
T1-770.t: 부터 is mainly for time; for places use 에서: 서울에서 부산까지.

T1-771.forms: time/place + 까지 (다섯 시까지, 부산까지) · 부터/에서 … 까지
T1-771.e: Pairs with 부터: 월요일부터 금요일까지 = Monday through Friday.

T1-772.forms: same after consonant or vowel · A보다 B가 더 … (B is more … than A)
T1-772.e: Comes from 보다 (to see). 커피보다 차 = tea rather than coffee.
T1-772.t: As a particle it attaches directly to a noun.

T1-901.x: Shall we order fried chicken for dinner tonight?
T1-901.e: From English 'chicken', but in Korean it means fried chicken; chicken meat is 닭고기.
T1-901.t: Can't decide? Order 반반: half 후라이드 (plain fried), half 양념 (sweet and spicy sauce).

T1-9001.x: Hmm, I'll go with the bibimbap.
T1-9001.e: Sound word for thinking, like English 'hmm'.
T1-9001.t: In texts it is written 음… or 흠. Don't confuse it with 음 (音) 'sound', as in 음악.
